findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-060-005: T5 as a whole reveals that this characteristic has an eschatological orientation as its formative telos. The formation arc moves from constitutive endowment (Spirit and wisdom given to form inner-bein…
findings.finding_value: T5 as a whole reveals that this characteristic has an eschatological orientation as its formative telos. The formation arc moves from constitutive endowment (Spirit and wisdom given to form inner-being capacity) through sustained covenantal narrative (the memory of received giving as formation environment) through suffering-testing (revealing whether inner-being giving is genuine) toward eschatological fullness ("oaks of righteousness," total communal transformation). The mechanisms are plural and context-specific — encounter (covenantal), gradual formation (endowing), sovereign reversal (eschatological) — revealing that formation is not a single pathway but a multi-modal process. The suffering relation is analytically significant: the characteristic is suffering-tested (revealed in human direction) and suffering-responsive (triggered in divine direction), showing that suffering is not incidental to the formation process but an integral context. T5.7 closes formally — no constitutional body deposit. What T5 reveals as a whole: faithfulness-as-giving is constitutively developmental — its present forms anticipate and move toward a fullness that is not yet fully realised. Every giving is, in some sense, an eschatological act: it participates in the pattern of divine giving that is moving toward total, permanent, communal transformation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-004: The working description of the characteristic (T1.2.3, Q&A-018) — faithfulness as an inner-being quality that enacts commitments, orientations, and compassions through giving — is directly illuminated…
findings.finding_value: The working description of the characteristic (T1.2.3, Q&A-018) — faithfulness as an inner-being quality that enacts commitments, orientations, and compassions through giving — is directly illuminated by T5's formation account. The working description names a state of the person; T5 reveals how that state is produced and where it is oriented. Specifically: the sustained inner-being effects (T1.6: trust, praise orientation, responsiveness, cognitive formation) are precisely the formation arc outcomes of T5. Sustained covenantal giving produces identity as recipients of promise (T5.5); endowing giving constitutes cognitive capacity (T5.3); eschatological giving produces the endpoint state of "oaks of righteousness" (T5.6). What this pair reveals: the working definition of the characteristic is not a static description but an arc description — it names the person being formed toward a fullness that is not yet complete. The characteristic is definitionally developmental.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-009: The constitutional movement patterns (T2.10 — constitutive spirit→mind, expressive inner→body, transformative outside-in→inside renewed→inside-out) directly correspond to the formation mechanisms (T5.…
findings.finding_value: The constitutional movement patterns (T2.10 — constitutive spirit→mind, expressive inner→body, transformative outside-in→inside renewed→inside-out) directly correspond to the formation mechanisms (T5.3 — gradual formation, encounter/event, sovereign reversal). The constitutive movement (spirit→mind) corresponds to the gradual-formation mechanism: Spirit given to instruct forms inner capacity over time through repeated constitutional deepening. The expressive movement (inner→body) corresponds to the encounter/event mechanism: the covenantal giving event produces an immediate inner-to-outer response (altar-building). The transformative movement (outside-in→inside renewed→inside-out) corresponds to sovereign reversal: the eschatological giving reaches in and renews, then the renewed inner life expresses outward (praise). What this pair reveals: constitutional movement and formative mechanism are two descriptions of the same transformative process. The characteristic forms the person through the constitutional pathways by which it moves — formation is constitutional movement over time.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-016: The relational interfaces (T4 — divine-initiative, human-responsive, covenantal scope) and the formation arc (T5 — constitutive endowment, sustained narrative, eschatological orientation) reveal that …
findings.finding_value: The relational interfaces (T4 — divine-initiative, human-responsive, covenantal scope) and the formation arc (T5 — constitutive endowment, sustained narrative, eschatological orientation) reveal that formation happens through relational interfaces. The God-to-human interface is the channel through which constitutive formation occurs (Spirit given, wisdom deposited — T5.5). The human-to-God interface is both the goal of formation (glory-giving as the proper orientation of the formed person) and a constituent of the formation process (practising glory-giving forms the person who gives glory). What this pair reveals: formation is not an individual inner process — it is a relational event. The person is not formed in isolation from God and others; they are formed through the giving and receiving that constitutes the relational interfaces. The formation arc (T5) is the temporal dimension of the relational structure (T4): what the interfaces do over time is formation.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-060-020: The formation arc (T5 — developmental, eschatologically oriented, suffering-tested) and the methodological analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, diverges on received-constitutive character; Hos 11…
findings.finding_value: The formation arc (T5 — developmental, eschatologically oriented, suffering-tested) and the methodological analysis (T7 — virtue ethics illuminates, diverges on received-constitutive character; Hos 11:8 as primary anchor) produce a pointed finding. The virtue ethics framework (T7.3.2) illuminates the formation arc well — disposition formed through repeated enacted commitment toward stable character — but diverges at the key point: virtue ethics assumes the person generates virtue through practice, while the biblical account places constitutive divine giving (Spirit, wisdom) as the prior condition of formative capacity (T5.5, T2.1). The divergence maps exactly onto the T5 finding that formation is constitutively dependent on received divine giving. Hos 11:8 as primary anchor (T7.2.5) is also the key verse for the formation arc: divine compassion overriding judicial logic is itself a formative act — it preserves the relational context within which human formation can continue. What this pair reveals: the evidential and methodological analysis (T7) independently identifies the same structural priority that the formation analysis (T5) finds: the constitutive primacy of divine giving as the ground of human formation.

Both. In the disordered register: hatred transforms the person's condition by progressively narrowing the inner life around the object of hatred. Gen 37:4-8 shows the transformation unfolding in steps — each provocation deepens the hatred ("they hated him even more"), and what begins as a response to perceived favouritism settles into an inner organising principle that makes peaceful speech impossible and leads eventually to the decision to sell Joseph into slavery. The person has not merely acquired an attitude; they have been reorganised differently inside. In the righteous register: hatred of evil transforms the person's orientation toward the entire moral landscape. Psa 45:7's language of anointing grounded in the inner orientation ("you have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God your God has anointed you") is formational language — the inner orientation has been shaped over time into a stable character quality.

Changes the person's condition — progressively establishing covenantal closure. Isa 1:4: "they have despised the Holy One of Israel, they are utterly estranged" — the estrangement is the sustained effect. Deu 31:20's predictive sequence (prosperity → contempt → covenant-breaking) shows contempt as a middle stage in a progressive deterioration. Contempt does not remain static; it advances the person's estrangement from what was once the ground of their life.

The most dramatic transformation in M06-C is the inversion visible in group 252-002: what begins as a moral capacity (the ability to abhor evil) undergoes a directional reversal — those who once might have abhorred evil now abhor justice. This inversion is not sudden; it is a progressive moral drift in which the inner constitution is gradually reorganised. The characteristic is not new — the capacity survives — but its direction has been reversed. The person has been transformed not by gaining something but by having something reoriented.

Cruelty produces transformation through the progressive removal of limiting inner goods. The person does not become cruel in a single moment; the character quality consolidates through sustained practice of acting without mercy and without setting God before themselves. Pro 12:10's "the mercy of the wicked is cruel" is the description of cruelty at its consolidated state — even mercy-attempts are shaped by the underlying character. The transformation is complete when every expression — including apparent mercy — is coloured by the cruelty.

Reproach produces transformation in both directions. In the negative direction: sustained reproach restructures the person's inner life — their perception of themselves (Psa 22:6), their relation to others (Psa 31:11), and their volitional capacity (Job 31:34). The condition becomes formative. In the positive direction: borne reproach — particularly reproach borne for God's sake — produces transformed capacity. 1Th 2:2: "we had boldness in our God to declare the gospel...in the midst of much conflict" — the experience of having been shamefully treated becomes the ground of a deeper boldness. The reproach has been passed through rather than destroyed by.

The adversary relationship transforms through the demands it makes: urgent decision (Mat 5:25), persistent appeal (Luk 18:3), active vigilance (1Pe 5:8). The transformation is the development of the inner resources required to face structured opposition — urgency, persistence, and sober watchfulness. The characteristic demands inner capacities that, when developed, form the person.

Malice transforms by reorganising the person's affective orientation around the pleasure of another's destruction. The "never-ending enmity" (Eze 25:15) names the self-perpetuating quality — the characteristic does not cycle down but renews itself, deepening the inner organisation around the malice as it finds satisfaction.

**[A1 — God Righteousness]** God's righteousness transforms the person who genuinely encounters it — by changing orientation first. Felix's alarm (Act 24:25, VSG M26-A1-006) shows an immediate re-orientation of inner posture (fear, recognition) without sustained transformation, because he chose not to receive the standard. The person who genuinely submits to God's righteousness — "you are righteous; we have sinned" (Neh 9:33; Dan 9:7, VSG M26-A1-006) — undergoes an orientation change that produces the condition for all other transformation: the acknowledgment that God's standard is the measure.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Both — condition and orientation. The condition changes: the person moves from non-righteous to righteous (or the reverse in Ezekiel's forfeiture model, Eze 18:24, VSG M26-A2-002). The orientation changes: the righteous person is oriented toward God (A2-014), toward others (A2-012), toward the future (A2-017). The NT transformation is the more comprehensive one: "born of him" (1Jo 2:29, VSG M26-A2-014) names a new-birth transformation — the deepest possible change of condition alongside a complete re-orientation of the person.

**[B — Moral Uprightness]** Primarily orientation. The change produced by uprightness is the inner directional alignment of the person toward what is straight. The path metaphor (Pro 2:13; 4:11, VSG 1211-002) is an orientation metaphor — the person is turned toward the path of uprightness. The condition that results (the person who walks in uprightness, Pro 14:2) is the sustained expression of the orientation change.

**[C — Justification]** Primarily condition — the person's standing before God changes from guilty to righteous. This is the most explicit condition-change in the cluster. However, it produces a secondary orientation change: the freed and justified person is oriented toward God as heir and toward continued righteous living ("go, and from now on sin no more," Joh 8:11; VSG 3194-001 context). The condition change (standing before God) precedes and enables the orientation change (heir-living).

**[D — Avenging Justice]** Primarily orientation — the transformation D produces is the re-orientation of the wronged person away from autonomous vengeance toward trust in God. "Leave it to the wrath of God" (Rom 12:19, VSG 6841-002) is an orientation change: the person's inner posture toward injustice is transformed from self-execution to entrusting. This orientation change produces the condition of non-retaliation.

**[E — Condemnation]** Both. Freedom from condemnation produces a condition change (from under-verdict to freed) and an orientation change (from guilt-weight to forward-movement: "go, and sin no more," Joh 8:11). The self-condemnation of autokatakritos (Tit 3:11, VSG 4848-001) is itself a condition — the condition of being under the self-verdict. Transformation requires something external to break that self-reinforcing condition.

**[F — Moral Reckoning]** Primarily orientation — the reckoning act re-orients the person toward the declared reality. "Count yourselves dead to sin and alive to God" (Rom 6:11, VSG 3410-001) — the counting changes how the person is oriented toward their own condition (dead to sin) and toward God (alive). This is an orientation change applied to an existing condition (the justified standing of C).

**[G — Structural Opposites]** Condition change — sustained wickedness changes the person's condition: the heart hardens (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001), the person accumulates wrath, the capacity to repent diminishes. This is a condition change in the wrong direction: the person becomes more firmly established in wickedness over time.

**[CLUSTER — T5.1]** E. The cluster produces transformation in both condition and orientation — but the sequence matters. The condition change of justification (C) precedes and enables the orientation changes (A2, B, D, F). The cluster's transformative arc is: God's righteousness proclaimed → encounter produces recognition (A1) → faith-response receives justification (C) → condition changed → orientation transforms throughout the inner life (A2 direction toward God and others, B uprightness-orientation, D trust-orientation, F reckoning-orientation). The G-path runs in reverse: wickedness hardens condition and progressively distorts orientation.

findings.finding_value: M01-A reverential fear produces transformation in both dimensions. It changes **orientation**: Exo 14:31 (Israel's witness of God's power over Egypt produces fear of the Lord and belief — the people's inner orientation shifts from terror of Egypt to reverent trust in God); Jon 1:16 (sailors' storm-terror converts into reverential worship — "fear becomes the inner ground of devotion" — a transformation of orientation from threat-directed to God-directed fear). It also produces change in **condition**: Pro 10:27 (fear of the Lord extending life — a condition-change); Pro 19:23 (fear leading to life and "restful inner satisfaction" — a settled new condition of security); Jer 32:40 (God implanting fear as a permanent disposition "preventing them from turning away" — a condition of inner stability replacing prior instability). Both dimensions are evidenced.

M01-B's commanded-release register (M01-B-VCG-06, anchor Isa 43:1) produces transformation in orientation: the person who receives "do not fear" moves from a grip of acute dread to a posture of trust grounded in divine presence. Dan 10:19 (M01-B-VCG-01: "fear is commanded away and replaced by peace and strength — the inner person moves from fearful weakness to fortified courage as the heavenly messenger speaks"). This is primarily **orientation-change** — the person's relationship to their threatening circumstance shifts without the circumstance itself changing.

M01-C's divinely deployed terror produces **condition-change** in enemy peoples: Gen 35:5 (God-sent terror paralysing the will of surrounding cities — their condition of active hostility becomes one of paralysis); Est 9:2-3 (dread of the Jews redirecting the will of provincial officials — their condition of opposition converts to active assistance). The condition of the enemy is transformed by the terror imposed.

M01-D dismay produces **condition-change** through its destructive dimension (inner collapse) and through its commanded-against-dismay corpus (M01-D-VCG-04): Jer 1:17 (the prophet commanded not to let dismay grip him — the implied transformation is from potential collapse to sustained composure grounded in divine commission). Dismay unchecked is a condition-worsening transformation; commanded against, it is resisted as the precondition of a transformed stable condition.

M01-E-VCG-02 (trembling at God's word, anchor Isa 66:2) produces transformation in orientation: those who tremble at God's word form a defined community whose orientation toward divine communication is permanently marked by reverential sobriety (Isa 66:5: their trembling reverence marks their identity and sets them apart, with God's vindication promised to this inner posture — an orientation-change producing a stable identity).

M01-F's primary transformative movement is from chronic anxiety to rest. Isa 12:2 (M01-F-VCG-04: "trust in God displacing dread from the inner person — the speaker declares that because God is his strength, fear no longer has a hold on his heart"); 1Jo 4:18 (M01-A-VCG-06/F-VCG-04: "perfect love expels fear entirely" — a transformation of inner condition in which the characteristic is removed). Psa 34:4 (anchor M01-F-VCG-02: "the psalmist sought the Lord and was delivered from all his fears — these fears were inner terrors and anxieties; divine response removed them entirely"). Both condition and orientation change.

M01-G's transformation is the spirit-level move from timidity to the spirit of power, love, and self-control (2Ti 1:7 anchor: the contrast implies that the gift of God's spirit displaces the spirit of timidity — a spirit-level condition-change). 2Ti 1:6 context (the call to stir up the gift) implies the transformation is not automatic but involves the person's own engagement.

M01 produces transformation in both condition and orientation across all sub-groups. The most consistent transformation pattern is: fear directed toward God (M01-A) produces stable new conditions (wisdom, life, security) and transformed orientations (from threat-directed to God-directed). Fear commanded away (M01-B-VCG-06) transforms orientation without necessarily changing circumstance. Chronic fear overcome (M01-F, G) transforms condition (from bondage to freedom). The cluster confirms that fear is formatively powerful in both directions — ordered fear builds the person up; unaddressed disordered fear tears the person down.

Yes. The corpus evidences transformation in both directions. (1) Transformation of condition: God transforms mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11 — M03-B-VCG-03 anchor), sorrow into joy (Jer 31:13 — M03-B-VCG-02), weeping into morning joy (Psa 30:5 — M03-A-VCG-04). These are transformations of the person's condition — the grief state is replaced by joy. (2) Transformation of orientation: godly grief produces earnestness, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and readiness to see justice done — reshaping the inner landscape rather than simply ending the grief (2Cor 7:11 — M03-C-VCG-02). This is transformation of the person's inner orientation through the grief rather than merely beyond it.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. Psa 16:9's "flesh also dwells secure" shows the inner exultation producing a transformed bodily state — security and ease replacing anxiety. Psa 51:8's hoped-for restoration of rejoicing in "bones that you have broken" would represent a transformation from brokenness to restored vitality. Hab 3:18's "yet I will rejoice" in total material loss represents a transformation of inner condition despite unchanged external circumstances — the exultation produces an altered relationship to the circumstances rather than altered circumstances.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes. Primary evidence: (1) **Mourning to dancing** — Psa 30:11 ("you have turned for me my mourning into dancing; you have clothed me with gladness") — the person's inner-being state is fundamentally transformed by God through Joy; (2) **Sorrow to Joy** — Joh 16:20 ("your sorrow will turn into joy"); Jer 31:13 ("I will turn their mourning into joy") — a categorical inner-being reversal; (3) **Anxiety displaced** — Phili 4:4–7 (commanded Joy in the Lord produces the peace that surpasses understanding — Joy transforms the anxious inner state into peace); (4) **Poverty-to-generosity** — 2Cor 8:2 (joy in extreme poverty overflowing into generosity — the characteristic transforms the self-protective posture of poverty into outward-directed giving); (5) **Fear to peace** — Luk 2:10 (the angel's announcement of Joy accompanies "fear not" — Joy displaces fear).

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, significantly: (1) **Character formation through trials** — Jas 1:2–4 (counting trials as joy → the testing of faith → steadfastness → completeness and wholeness) — Suffering-Joy is the enabling inner posture that allows trials to accomplish their full formative work; (2) **Freedom from circumstantial-dependence** — 2Cor 6:10 (adjacent — "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing") — the person formed by Suffering-Joy is transformed from one whose inner state mirrors external conditions to one whose inner life is constitutionally Spirit-anchored; (3) **Eschatological deepening** — 1Pe 4:13 ("that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed") — present Suffering-Joy transforms the inner person toward the eschatological state of unqualified joy; (4) **Crisis-to-faith** — Act 16:34 (the jailer's crisis of the earthquake → coming to faith → rejoicing) — the most dramatic transformation instance in the corpus.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes: (1) **Good news transforming inner state** — Pro 12:25 (anxiety → gladness through good word); Pro 15:30 (weariness/desire → refreshment through good news); 1Sa 16:23 (Saul: torment → refreshed and well through music); (2) **Testimony transforming communal inner state** — Neh 2:18 (discouragement → resolve through hearing God's good hand); (3) **Divine declaration transforming status** — makarismos (Rom 4:6, 9 — the divine declaration of blessedness transforms the inner status of the one to whom God counts righteousness); (4) **Moral evaluation convicting and transforming** — Eze 36:31 (recognition of "not good" deeds → self-loathing → the beginning of restored conscience).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in multiple registers: (1) **Will aligned through Delight** — Psa 37:4 ("delight yourself in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart") — the will's desires are transformed by Delight in God; (2) **Law internalized** — Psa 40:8 ("your law is within my heart") — the law's location changes from external to internal through Delight; (3) **Covenantal identity transformed** — Isa 62:4 (Zion renamed "My Delight Is in Her" — her identity transformed by being the object of divine Delight); (4) **Soul formed around object** — Isa 66:3 (soul delighting in abominations — the person's deepest self formed around the wrong object through sustained misdirected Delight); (5) **Adversity-surviving resilience** — Psa 119:92 (Delight in the law sustaining through affliction — the inner person transformed into one capable of enduring without perishing).

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes: (1) **Pro 16:24** — gracious-word Pleasure producing "sweetness to the soul and health to the body" — a holistic transformative healing effect on the whole person; (2) **Gen 8:21** — God's inner Pleasure at Noah's offering producing a divine resolve ("I will never again curse the ground") — the soothing aroma transforms God's stated disposition toward the fallen world; (3) **Psa 27:4** — sustained dwelling in God's house and gazing on his beauty produces transformation toward that beauty; (4) **Job 36:11** — listening and serving God producing "years in pleasantness" — transformation of life-quality through the obedient posture; (5) **Deu 28:54, 56** — the reverse: loss of Pleasure under the curse transforms the character of daily life and inner experience.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes: (1) **Job's restoration** — Job 42:3 ("things too wonderful for me, which I did not know") — Wonder at God's incomprehensibility produces Job's restored inner posture; the divine whirlwind-encounter producing Wonder-humility is the hinge of Job's transformation from complaint to restored relationship; (2) **Psa 119:129** — "your testimonies are wonderful; therefore my soul keeps them" — Wonder in God's law producing obedient keeping; (3) **Mar 1:27** — the crowd's transformation from the routine synagogue assembly into a questioning, astonished community encountering something utterly new; (4) **The anti-type — Neh 9:17** — wonder-failure producing the transformation from covenant people into rebels; the failure to wonder precedes and enables the moral transformation toward rebellion.

The orientation-change is the more fundamental transformation: the community's inner directional commitment has been redirected.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Both condition and orientation. (1) *Condition change*: 2Ki 8:20 / 2Ch 21:8 — "Edom revolted... and set up a king of their own" — the political condition is permanently transformed: from vassal to independent kingdom. The governing relationship is changed by the revolt's decisive act. 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion to this day" — the political-covenantal condition is permanently altered from unified Davidic kingdom to divided. (2) *Orientation change*: the revolting community reorients its political allegiance from the prior governing authority to its own self-governance. 2Ch 21:10 — the spiritual-political orientation of Jehoram (forsaking the Lord) produces the reorientation of Edom and Libnah away from Judah's governing authority. Both condition (the political relationship) and orientation (the political allegiance) are transformed by revolt.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Both, with the form determining the depth. (1) *Condition change*: Mat 12:31 — "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" — a permanent change in the person's moral-spiritual condition before God; the unforgivable blasphemy produces an irreversible condition of un-forgiven-ness. Mar 14:64 — "they all condemned him as deserving death" — the blasphemy-verdict produces the condition of the condemned. (2) *Orientation change*: 2Ti 3:2 — the blasphemous/abusive character as a settled end-times disposition — the practitioner's orientation has been formed around the sinful speech pattern. 1Ti 6:4 — the craving for controversy deepens through the slander it generates, reorienting the person further toward sinful speech. 1Ti 1:13's reversal — blasphemer → apostle through mercy — shows that orientation can be transformed in the positive direction.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows that wickedness-as-settled-person-identity produces two types of transformation: (1) internal constitutional transformation — the sustained operation of the characteristic progressively consolidates the person's inner orientation and deepens their moral blindness (Pro 4:19 — deepening darkness; Isa 26:10 — incorrigibility under grace; Dan 12:10 — inability to understand at the eschatological moment). Both condition (the person's inner state — from partial to total moral closure) and orientation (the directional bent of the will — deepening away from God) are transformed. (2) The reversible transformation of the wicked person who turns: the Ezekiel corpus (VCG-07, Eze 18:21-27; 33:12-19) documents a transformation of orientation (the will turns from wickedness to justice) that produces a transformation of condition (life rather than death). The characteristic thus produces transformations in both directions depending on whether the volitional dynamic is hardening (deepening the characteristic) or reversing it (departing from it).

**[CHAR-2]** E — The characteristic produces transformation primarily in the person's condition rather than orientation moment-by-moment. The tree-nature metaphor (Mat 7:17-18 — VCG-02) frames the characteristic as a condition — the diseased tree's condition determines its fruit. Transformation of the condition is what the evidence calls for: Heb 10:22 (vc=14426 — VCG-06) — the evil conscience sprinkled clean is a transformation of the conscience's constitutional condition; Act 3:26 (vc=14410 — VCG-05) — turning from wickedness through divine blessing is a transformation of the inner orientation away from the constitutional evil; Jam 1:21 (vc=14368 — VCG-05) — stripping away rampant wickedness and receiving the implanted word changes both the condition (emptied of the rampant wickedness) and the orientation (receptive to the word). The evidence shows the characteristic producing transformation of condition primarily, with consequent reorientation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The characteristic produces transformation of both condition and orientation, depending on direction. In the deepening direction: sustained commission of abomination transforms the inner condition (conscience increasingly silenced — Jer 6:15; 8:12 — VCG-04 — "did not know how to blush") and the inner orientation (Pro 13:19 — vc=1687 — VCG-05: the will so bonded to evil that turning from it is experienced as abominable). In the redemptive direction: when memory is restored (Eze 36:31 — vc=1681 — VCG-04: "then you will remember… and you will loathe yourselves"), both condition (conscience reactivated) and orientation (self-loathing replacing self-justification) are transformed. Eze 14:6 (vc=65984 — VCG-04): "repent and turn away from your idols, and turn away your faces from all your abominations" — the commanded turning transforms both orientation (the will's direction) and condition (the person who has turned is no longer oriented toward abomination).

**[CHAR-4]** E — The characteristic produces transformation of both condition and orientation. Hos 9:10 (vc=1632 — VCG-04): "they became detestable like the thing they loved" — condition is transformed: the person's own inner character-quality shifts toward the image of what they worship. Eze 11:21 (vc=1631/65982 — VCG-05): "heart goes after their detestable things" — orientation is transformed: the heart's directional faculty is re-oriented toward idols. The progressive deepening evidence (Eze 8:13; 8:15 — VCG-05: "still greater abominations") shows both condition (progressively more corrupted) and orientation (progressively more firmly directed toward idols) transforming together over time. The Ezekiel restoration (Eze 37:23 — VCG-05) also documents transformation of both condition ("I will save them and cleanse them") and orientation ("they shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols").

**[CHAR-5]** E — The characteristic produces transformation of both condition and orientation. Condition: Psa 36:3 (vc=38234 — VCG-04): "he has ceased to act wisely and do good" — the person's condition shifts from wisdom-capable to wisdom-displaced; Pro 30:20 (vc=38222 — VCG-04): the conscience-deadened state is a transformed condition. Orientation: Psa 119:133 (vc=38227 — VCG-04): iniquity seeking dominion — the will's orientation progressively conforms to iniquity's direction; Pro 17:4 (vc=38219 — VCG-03): the evildoer's inner ear preferentially oriented toward wicked lips — an orientation-transformation. The transformative arc documented in T2.8.1 (worn inner path, conscience silenced) shows both condition (what the person is capable of) and orientation (what direction they face) being reshaped by sustained iniquity.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The characteristic produces transformation of both condition and orientation in VCG-01. Rev 16:9 → 16:11 → 16:21 (VCG-01): the sequence across three plague events shows progressive solidification — the will's anti-God orientation becomes more fixed, the condition of hardness deepens. The orientation is transformed in the direction of entrenched defiance: from potentially responding to judgment (initial contact) toward the settled state of cursing as reflex response. Condition: Jude 10 (vc=14355 — VCG-01): "destroyed by all that they, like unreasoning animals, understand instinctively" — the sustained characteristic produces a condition of self-destruction through sub-rational instinct: the person's constitutional condition is being destroyed by what they do not understand. For VCG-03's targets: the falsely accused's condition is one of maintained good conscience (1Pe 3:16 — VCG-03) — the counter-formation.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics produce transformation in both condition and orientation — confirmed unanimously across the cluster. The cluster's transformative pattern is consistently in the direction of deepening: each characteristic, when sustained, progressively transforms both what the person is capable of (condition) and what direction they face (orientation), moving both in the direction of the respective evil-form. Char 4 provides the most concentrated transformation evidence: Hos 9:10 — "became detestable like the thing they loved" — the person is constitutionally transformed toward the image of their idolatrous object. Char 6 provides the most extreme orientation transformation: Rev 16:9/11/21 — the will's anti-God orientation becomes progressively more fixed under each successive judgment. Chars 1 and 5 share the worn-path transformation (Job 22:15 — the old way that wicked men have trod — habituation deepening the moral trajectory). All six characteristics show transformation as an active consequence of sustained possession rather than a static condition.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, the characteristic produces transformation in the person's condition. The defilement-state is a condition-change: from clean to unclean (at acquisition) and from unclean to clean again (at resolution). The entire remedial system — washing, waiting, examination, water of impurity — is a structured sequence of condition-transformation. The transformation is primarily of the person's condition (their sacral standing within the covenant community), not of their deeper character or orientation per se. However, the orientation is also transformed in the formative register: sustained engagement with the clean/unclean system over a lifetime forms the person's orientation toward sacral vigilance, as evidenced in Peter's Act 10:14 conviction (M10c-B-VCG-05) — his orientation has been transformed by a lifetime of categorical formation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in both directions: the defilement-state transforms the person downward through progressive moral deterioration, and the call to cleansing represents a transformative reversal. The deterioration trajectory is documented at Rom 1:24 (VCG-02) — "gave them up to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies"; Rom 6:19 (VCG-02) — "lawlessness leading to more lawlessness"; Eph 4:19 (VCG-02) — "become callous... greedy to practice every kind of impurity." Each verse shows a different stage of a downward condition-transformation in the inner person. The reversal trajectory is named at 2Cor 7:1 (VCG-03) — "let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion" — a transformation in orientation from defilement to holiness. The characteristic thus produces transformation in both the person's condition (deteriorating) and their orientation (if the call is heeded, reversing toward holiness).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, in both directions. The characteristic transforms the community's condition downward (land contaminated, sanctuary desecrated, covenant severed, community expelled) and has a designed reversal in the eschatological register (Eze 37:23 — "they shall not defile themselves anymore"; Zec 13:1 — fountain of cleansing). The transformation of condition (land, sanctuary, divine name from holy to defiled) is thoroughly documented in VCGs -02, -03, -04. The transformation of orientation is evidenced in Eze 20:43 (VCG-02): the community will remember and loathe — their orientation toward their own past will be transformed from self-justifying denial (Jer 2:23) to self-loathing (Eze 20:43). Both condition-change and orientation-change are evidenced.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, in both directions. Downward transformation: the spirit's seizure transforms the person's condition comprehensively — will overridden (Luk 8:29), faculties suppressed (Mar 9:25), communal belonging severed (Mar 5:2), bodily agency displaced (Luk 9:42). Upward restoration: the expulsion reverses the transformation — Luk 6:18 (VCG-02): "were cured"; Luk 9:42 (VCG-01): "healed the boy, and gave him back to his father"; Act 5:16 (VCG-02): "they were all healed." The characteristic changes the person's condition (defilement-state) and their communal orientation (given back to the father).

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics produce transformation, and all four produce transformation in both directions (downward into defilement and upward through restoration). The form of transformation differs by characteristic. Characteristic 1: primarily condition-transformation (from clean to defiled to restored-clean); also orientation-transformation through the formative register (sustained engagement with the categorical system shapes Peter's Act 10:14 conviction — a lifetime of orientation-change). Characteristic 2: both condition-transformation (the progressive deterioration trajectory: desire → judicial release → impurity → bodily dishonour → escalating lawlessness — Rom 1:24/6:19/Eph 4:19) and orientation-transformation (2Cor 7:1 — "bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God"). Characteristic 3: condition-transformation of the sacred environment (land contaminated, sanctuary desecrated, name defiled) and orientation-transformation (Jer 2:23 — self-justifying denial → Eze 20:43 — future self-loathing and repentance). Characteristic 4: condition-transformation (spirit-invasion transforming the person's whole constitutional state — will overridden, faculties suppressed) and restoration-transformation (Luk 6:18 — "cured"; Luk 9:42 — "gave him back to his father"). The cluster's unanimous transformation confirmation confirms the M10c domain as inherently dynamic — defilement is not a static background condition but a condition that transforms the person and their environment.

questions.question_text: Is the transformation reversible or irreversible in the evidence?

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides evidence for both possibilities, in different registers:

**Irreversible (divine forgiveness in new covenant register):** Jer 31:34 — "I will remember their sin no more." OBS-064-017: "the debt is not merely cancelled but rendered non-recallable." The permanence of the new covenant forgiveness points toward irreversibility — the cognitive claim is permanently terminated. The afesis state, once received through Christ's atonement, is presented as a completed and permanent condition (Eph 1:7 — "we have redemption").

**Reversible (under certain conditions):** Mat 18:35 — the parable shows forgiveness revoked: the servant's forgiveness was withdrawn when he refused to extend it. F-003 confirms this: "the servant who received enormous forgiveness and refused to extend it had his forgiveness revoked." This is a named case of reversal — the received forgiveness was not permanent under conditions of refusal to extend.

**Permanent foreclosure (outer limit):** Mar 3:29 — the unforgivable sin produces a state in which forgiveness is permanently inaccessible. This is not reversal of received forgiveness but permanent foreclosure of potential future reception.

*New finding:* The data implies a distinction between **formal receipt** of forgiveness (which may be revoked if not integrated at the heart level and expressed horizontally — Mat 18:35) and **deep covenant receipt** (which is rendered permanent and non-recallable — Jer 31:34). The reversibility question therefore depends on the depth and genuineness of the reception. This distinction between revocable formal receipt and irrevocable genuine receipt has not been assembled in existing observations and is analytically significant.

findings.session_b_note:
The data suggests irreversibility for the deepest transformations. charitoō (Luk 1:28: kecharitōmenē) is a perfect passive — completed act with continuing state. 1Cor 15:10 is framed in terms of being ("I am what I am") — implying a permanent condition. However, grace "received in vain" (2Cor 6:1, referenced in SD pointers) suggests not every grace-reception produces irreversible transformation. The question is not fully resolved.

*Gap identified: the reversibility question is partially addressed but not resolved.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data addresses reversibility indirectly through two contrasting lines of evidence:

**Reversibility evidenced (Lam 4:10):** The compassionate character quality (ra.cha.ma.ni) of the women in Lam 4:10 is violated under the extreme pressure of the siege. The character quality that defined them as compassionate persons was not proof against external catastrophe — it was violated, inverted, and forced into its opposite. This suggests that the transformation of character produced by compassion (becoming a compassionate person) is not irreversible under all conditions. Sufficient external pressure can force the violation of the deepest formed inner qualities.

**Durability evidenced (chesed vocabulary):** Lam 3:22 — "his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning." The everlasting chesed vocabulary names divine compassion as inherently irreversible on God's side — it does not cease, does not withdraw permanently, and does not fail. On the human side, the chasid type (the devout, chesed-embodying person) is presented as a stable character identity, not a momentary state.

**The Matt 18:35 parallel (from instruction T5.1 note):** The programme instruction notes Mat 18:35 as the primary reversibility data point for forgiveness. The compassion data does not contain an equivalent direct verse on reversibility. The unforgiving servant parable (Matt 18:27) shows the king's compassion (splanchnizō) producing debt-release, which is then effectively reversed by the servant's own failure to extend compassion. The structural implication: the transformation produced by received compassion can be forfeited if the recipient fails to embody what they have received. This is a significant finding — it places compassion within an integrated moral framework in which reception without corresponding character-formation does not hold.

findings.session_b_note:
The verse evidence does not directly address reversibility for contrition in the way that the forgiveness analysis addressed the Mat 18:35 reversibility question. What the data does show:

- The hardened posture of Jer 44:10 (those who have not humbled themselves even after extended opportunity) suggests that contrite orientation can be persistently withheld — which implies it is not automatically permanent once it has not been established.
- The Hithpael form "allowing oneself to be crushed" implies ongoing volitional involvement — which may imply the contrite condition requires ongoing volitional non-resistance rather than being a one-time irreversible change.

Whether a person who has been genuinely contrite can return to hardness is not directly addressed. The structural opposite (pride, hardness) is described as a present condition (Jer 44:10), not as a return from prior contrition.

*Partial: the data implies contrition involves ongoing volitional non-resistance (not automatically permanent); direct evidence on reversibility is absent.*

findings.session_b_note:
The data provides evidence in both directions.

**Toward irreversibility:** Jer 13:23 — the leopard's spots image. The group description reads: "indelibly formed inner moral character depicted as fixed marking." The fellowship-vocabulary (chavar root) is here applied to constitutional formation so thoroughgoing that reversal is presented as inconceivable. Character conformity through sustained fellowship (including evil fellowship) can become constitutionally fixed.

**Toward reversibility — the idolatrous joining:** Hos 4:17 — *Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone* — the divine abandonment of the idolatrously-joined person implies that the situation is reversible in principle (God could reclaim; abandonment is the current response to the misdirected joining), even if the immediate condition is one of spiritual bondage.

**The wound-healing pattern:** Pro 20:30 and Isa 53:5 — the wound-fellowship produces purification and healing. These are presented as genuine and completed changes, but the data does not address their permanence or reversibility.

**New finding:** The reversibility question for fellowship is object-dependent. Wrong fellowship that produces constitutional character fixity (Jer 13:23) tends toward irreversibility. Wound-fellowship that produces purification and healing may be more permanent in the positive direction. But the data does not resolve this distinction definitively. It is a Session D question.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence raises reversibility as a concern without fully resolving it. Rom 11:22 names a conditional dimension: "provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off." The use of "cut off" implies that the relational experience of divine goodness can be lost — which implies some form of reversibility in the human's receipt of goodness's benefits. However, this addresses the ongoing experience of chrēstotēs rather than the Spirit-level character transformation. Whether Spirit-produced goodness (agathōsunē and chrēstotēs as fruit) can be reversed is not directly addressed. The distinction between the character transformation (Spirit-produced inner quality) and the relational experience (ongoing receipt of divine chrēstotēs) is analytically important for this question, and the data does not fully resolve it. This is a genuine partial gap — formal vs genuine receipt distinction is not drawn in the evidence. (OBS-067-OBS-043, OBS-067-OBS-044, SP-067-018)

findings.finding_value: Love's formation operates through a multi-layered process in the data. The primary pathway is receptive: divine love received (1Jo 4:19) → Spirit infusion (Rom 5:5, Gal 5:22) → heart-reception → soul-response → community expression. Secondary pathways: obedience → soul purification → sincere love (1Pe 1:22); forgiveness received → love generated (Luk 7:47 — via SD-020); training within community (Tit 2:4). Love can grow (1Th 3:12) and increase through the Lord's action. Its reversibility is asymmetric: divine love is irreversible by nature (Jer 31:3 — everlasting; Lam 3:22 — never ceasing); human love is subject to redirection through competing love-allegiances (2Ti 4:10 — Demas). The eschatological trajectory is toward perfection and direct knowledge: partial now (mediated by community, neighbour-teaching), moving toward fullness (perfect love casting out fear — 1Jo 4:18; direct divine knowledge — Jer 31:34; pleasures forevermore — Psa 16:11). Formation requires community — love cannot be formed in isolation; it requires both the divine giver and the human community as the formation context.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-103-019: The formation process and the structural relationships are mutually reinforcing systems. The formation pathway (divine love received → Spirit infusion → soul purification → community expression) maps …
findings.finding_value: The formation process and the structural relationships are mutually reinforcing systems. The formation pathway (divine love received → Spirit infusion → soul purification → community expression) maps onto the sequential structural position: love's formation follows the same sequence as love's structural position in the programme — first received (downstream of divine action), then formed (mediating), then expressed (generative of ethical life). The growth-capacity of love (1Th 3:12 — Q&A-092) explains the programme's most puzzling co-occurrence finding: strength and authority (C20, 105 and 69 shared verses respectively). Love growing under the Lord's enabling encounters contexts of power — covenantal love among the people of God is exercised within structures of authority, governance, and strength. The love-power co-occurrence reflects the formation context: love formed within communities is formed within structures of authority. The eschatological trajectory (toward perfect love and direct knowledge) describes the structural relationships' completion: when love reaches its eschatological form, the partial sequential relationships (love received → love given → ethical life) are resolved into the direct love-knowledge of the new covenant (Jer 31:34).

findings.session_b_note: The evidence distinguishes formal from genuine transformation. The covenant promise (Heb 8:12 — "I will remember their sins no more") names irreversible divine memory-erasure under the new covenant — the propitious act is permanent in its divine dimension. However, the *lo ruchamah* warning (Hos 1:6 — OBS-111-058) shows that mercy can be withdrawn in response to persistent covenant rejection — this is not the reversal of a completed atoning act but the suspension of the mercy relationship before or without that act. The Mat 18:34–35 parable (the unforgiving servant handed over to the jailer) raises questions about the stability of received mercy when inner transformation has not occurred — but this is parabolic and its resolution is not fully settled in the data. OBS-111-035, OBS-111-055, OBS-111-058.

findings.finding_value: Reading T5 as a whole reveals mercy's formative character: it is not static but inherently developmental and generative. The T5 synthesis: mercy produces dual transformation (objective condition + subjective orientation simultaneously); it moves persons through named inner-state sequences (at least four distinct sequences, Q&A-128); its mechanism is always specific, embodied, and costly; suffering is both the context that generates mercy-seeking and the formation-medium through which mercy-capacity deepens (Q&A-135); mercy functions as the first and foundational inner garment in the character formation sequence (Q&A-138); and mercy has an eschatological trajectory (future fullness in which the mercy-relationship is complete and permanent). T5.7 closed (no constitutional body deposit). The overarching T5 finding: mercy is a characteristic that is received, then forms the person into one who can receive it more deeply and extend it more genuinely — it has an inherent developmental arc.

The divine reviving of spirit and heart (Isa 57:15) may be reversible if the person subsequently hardens. The data does not explicitly address reversibility. OBS-030-028, OBS-030-047.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-005: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's stan…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's standing AND orientation-change in his reception of identity). Second, the formative cycle is self-reinforcing: the after-state of compassion-received feeds back into the before-state of compassion-readiness in the future — the person who has received compassion becomes more capable of extending it. Third, compassion plays a dual role in the sanctification arc: it is simultaneously the character target being formed (the person becoming compassionate over time) and the motivational ground that makes the formative relationship survivable through failure and return. Matthew 18:27 introduces the most critical formative warning: received compassion can be forfeited by failure to extend it — compassion is not a permanently possessed gift but a participatory moral framework. Three distinct mechanisms of change operate across contexts: encounter/sudden (splanchnizō — the moment of being moved), covenantal-sustaining/gradual (chesed — the steady faithfulness over time), and participatory-ontological (2Pe 1:4 pattern — sharing in what God is). T5.7 is formally closed: no body deposit established. All four relationships between suffering and compassion are evidenced — suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-011: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation pr…
findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation process from single compassion-event to compassion-character is the most important untraced developmental relationship in the registry. T5 provides the directional finding (the formative cycle feeds back from after-state to before-state) and names the three mechanisms (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological). T1 provides the definitional starting point (compassion as character quality is the endpoint of formation). Together they frame an arc that is identified but not filled: how does the moment of splanchnizō (T1 inner-event) accumulate into the settled character of ra.chum (T1 character quality)? T5's mechanisms suggest the answer but the data does not trace the path explicitly — a gap confirmed by both tiers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-016: T2's four-stage constitutional movement (somatic arousal → soul → volition → action) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) ar…
findings.finding_value: T2's four-stage constitutional movement (somatic arousal → soul → volition → action) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally complementary. T2 describes the movement within a single compassion-event; T5 describes how that event accumulates into character over time. The encounter/sudden mechanism (T5) corresponds to the full four-stage sequence of T2 in a single instance. The covenantal-sustaining mechanism (T5) corresponds to the repeated operation of the somatic-soul pathway (T2.2 — soul-level chesed as the sustaining character) over time. The participatory-ontological mechanism (T5) corresponds to the constitutional direction T2 identifies but leaves at spirit-level gap: if the deepest formation is participatory-ontological, the spirit-level dimension (T2.1 — entirely silent) may be where this operates — a convergent gap from two tiers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-020: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connecte…
findings.finding_value: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connected. T5 names compassion as the motivational ground that makes the sanctification arc survivable through failure and return — but T3 has already established that affect is the mechanism of this motivational ground: the character formation that T5 describes is accomplished through the affective mechanism that T3 identifies. The person who is formed into compassionate character (T5) is the person whose affective faculty has been trained to respond immediately and morally to perceived suffering (T3). T3's finding that affect and moral action are unified is T5's mechanism of formation: the person becoming compassionate is the person in whom the affective-moral unity is deepening and stabilising.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. T4's relational architecture and T5's formation mechanisms are the same structural reality described from relational and developmental perspectives respectively.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-026: T5's three mechanisms of change explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The encounter/sudden mechanism (splanchnizō producing immediate transformation) corresponds to t…
findings.finding_value: T5's three mechanisms of change explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The encounter/sudden mechanism (splanchnizō producing immediate transformation) corresponds to the high co-occurrence with despair (28 verses) and distress (16 verses) — these are the conditions that trigger the sudden compassion-event. The covenantal-sustaining mechanism corresponds to the high co-occurrence with love (196 verses), mercy (76 verses), and covenant (17 verses) — these are the characteristics that share the sustaining, gradual register with chesed. The participatory-ontological mechanism corresponds to the sequential relationship (compassion → mercy confirmed as constitutionally causal in T6.2) — the deepest formation mechanism produces the person who naturally extends mercy as the externalised form of the compassion-character formed within. Formation mechanisms (T5) explain co-occurrence patterns (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-005: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outp…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outpouring (Zec 12:10), word (Act 20:32 — grace operating through the proclaimed word), inference (Rom 8:32 — cognitive reasoning from the supreme grace-event to present assurance), and mediated-transformation (grace → tenderheartedness → forgiving — Eph 4:32, SD030). Five distinct mechanisms for a single characteristic is unique in the programme data. The creaturely recognition response (fear → mourning → prostration) is confirmed as a consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences across different evidential contexts — not incidental detail but structural feature. Suffering's relationship to grace is precisely distinguished: grace inhabits suffering rather than suffering producing grace (2Cor 12:9 — weakness as theatre of grace, not as generator of grace). The reversibility question (T5.1 P2) is the most significant gap: not fully resolved. The eschatological trajectory (T5.6) is evidenced through Eph 2:7 ("the immeasurable riches of his grace in the coming ages") and charitoō's perfect-passive form (completed state with continuing effect). T2.8 remains open; T5.7 is formally left open accordingly.

findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect finding (immediate/sustained contrast as qualitative, not merely temporal — what grace does immediately is creaturely recognition; what it does over time is constitution of identity and character) maps onto T5's formation mechanisms. The encounter mechanism (T5) produces the immediate effects named in T1.5; the word, inference, and mediated-transformation mechanisms (T5) produce the sustained effects of T1.6. T5's five mechanisms collectively explain how the four kinds named in T1.2 are produced across different temporal and contextual registers: disposition-receipt is the encounter mechanism; standing is the spirit-outpouring mechanism; capacity is the mediated-transformation mechanism; character quality is the sustained word-and-inference mechanism. T1 names what is produced; T5 names how each kind is produced.

findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (SD021 sequence: disposition → standing → capacity → character) and T5's five formation mechanisms describe the same formation arc from spatial and temporal perspectives. T2 identifies the constitutional levels through which grace moves; T5 identifies the mechanisms by which grace moves through each level in different contexts. The encounter mechanism (T5 — sudden specific relational event) produces the spirit-level reception (T2.1 — the initial point of arrival). The word mechanism (T5 — Act 20:32 — grace through proclaimed word) produces the soul-standing establishment (T2.2 — the word's sustained effect on the person's constitutive condition). The mediated-transformation mechanism (T5 — tenderheartedness → forgiving — Eph 4:32, SD030) corresponds to T2.7's bidirectional body-soul finding: the inner transformation mediates outward through the body-soul interface. T2.8's open question (body deposit) and T5.7's open status are formally aligned — both pending further investigation.

findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences) is the affective-faculty event (T3.4) at the moment of grace-arrival, which then constitutes the volitional-faculty alignment (T3.6 — the agency-constituting paradox) that enables the conscientious expression (T3.10). T5's formation arc (sustained work producing character-quality) is the longitudinal development of T3.9's finding (conscience operating fully within grace) into T3.10's finding (conscientiousness as the integrated moral character that grace constitutes over time). The person who has been formed by grace through the T5 formation arc is the person in whom T3's faculty engagements have been progressively deepened and integrated.

findings.finding_value: T5's most distinctive formation finding (five mechanisms, creaturely recognition response as consistent transitional state, grace inhabiting rather than resolving suffering) is grounded in and confirmed by T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The NT coinage charitoō (T7.1 P9 — coined for standing-in-favour as completed, continuing state) is the lexical ground of T5.1's irreversibility finding: the perfect passive grammatical form encodes precisely the "transformation not reversed" character that T5.1 identifies. T7.2's argument structure analysis (Zec 12:10 — grace outpoured → recognition → mourning → supplication) is the textual grounding for T5.2's creaturely recognition response finding: the sequence is not an incidental narrative feature but an argued structural pattern. T7.3's framework divergence (human science frameworks assuming prior capacity; Scripture denying it at the point of maximum incapacity — Eph 2:1-5) is the methodological expression of T5.5's deepest formation finding: the person cannot initiate their own formation by grace. T5 and T7 describe the same formation reality from narrative and lexical angles.

findings.session_b_note: The evidence points in different directions for different covenantal modes. (1) The new covenant constitutional transformation (law on heart, Spirit-administration) — the evidence does not explicitly address reversibility for this mode. The language is declarative and permanent in intent: God says "I will" (future promise framing in Jer 31:31-34; Heb 8:8-10 — OBS-034-040). The covenant is described as "eternal" (Heb 13:20 — OBS-034-074), which implies irreversibility. (2) Covenant-breach as reversible rupture: the OT evidence shows covenant breach (Dan 9:11 — OBS-034-036) followed by potential restoration (God's own covenant-memory persists despite breach — Gen 9:15, Lk 1:72 — OBS-034-073). Covenant is broken but not permanently destroyed from God's side. (3) Heb 10:29 (OBS-034-070): "trampled underfoot the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified" — this language implies that profaning the covenant after receiving it represents a severe and serious condition, though the text does not explicitly define the limits of reversibility. Gap: the question of whether new covenant transformation is individually reversible is not directly answered in the programme's verse set. Noting as P.

findings.session_b_note: The data shows both: (1) Reversible: Jer 16:5 ("I have taken away my peace from this people") — God can withdraw peace, reversing the relational condition; Psa 85:8 ("let them not turn back to folly") — the covenant condition of peace can be forfeited through turning; the human person can move from peace to peacelessness through rebellion; (2) Irreversible (covenantal): Isa 54:10 ("my covenant of peace shall not be removed") — the eschatological covenant of peace is explicitly declared irrevocable by God's unilateral commitment; (3) Irreversible (accomplished): Eph 2:14-16 — Christ's peace-making through the cross is a completed historical act; the dividing wall has been broken down — this cannot be re-erected from the human side. The data distinguishes between experiential peace (reversible, depending on human orientation and divine response to sin) and covenantal/accomplished peace (irreversible, grounded in God's identity and Christ's cross).

findings.session_b_note: The eschatological transformations (Isa 61:3, Hos 2:15) are presented as permanent and final — "oaks of righteousness," "everlasting name" (Isa 56:5), "everlasting covenant" (Isa 61:8). The language of eschatological giving uses permanent-state vocabulary, suggesting irreversibility. The covenantal giving of land is presented as permanently intended ("everlasting possession," Gen 17:8) but historically the people lose the land (Jer 17:4 — "you shall loosen your hand from your heritage that I gave you") — suggesting that even given-land can be forfeited. The gap: the data does not clearly distinguish whether the reversibility of loss (land forfeited) represents a reversal of the transformation or a suspension of one mode of giving while another (judicial giving-over) replaces it. Partial answer: eschatological giving appears irreversible; covenantal giving of material goods appears conditionally reversible.

In the disordered register: no verse in M06-A describes a person moving from sustained hatred of a person to love or reconciliation using these terms. The transformation hatred produces appears highly resistant to reversal. Eschatologically: Psa 81:15 shows that the person whose defining inner orientation is hatred of God will "cringe toward him" at the final horizon — that is exposure and collapse, not reconciliation. The fate "lasts forever."

The eschatological reversal is from the outside: Isa 60:14 — "all who despised you shall bow down at your feet." The contemner's inner reversal is not described; it is the external reversal of their position that is named.

The eschatological permanence of de.ra.on (Dan 12:2, Isa 66:24) implies irreversibility at the final horizon. The righteous abhorrence of evil reaches its completion; the condition of being permanently abhorrent cannot be undone.

Pro 11:17's implication (the kind man is the alternative to the cruel man) suggests reversal is possible in principle. But no M06-D verse describes a person moving from cruelty to mercy — the movement described is always cruelty toward its consequences and eventual removal.

Reversible by divine action: Jos 5:9 — God rolled it away in a moment. But deep reproach requires active forgetting (Isa 54:4) — restoration must actively address what reproach has deposited in memory and identity.

The pattern across M05: divine transformation is irreversible (love everlasting, mercy sovereign, reconciliation from God's side permanent); human practice-based transformation is potentially reversible (good conscience can be wrecked — 1Ti 1:19 — Group 1097; fellowship can be disrupted by walking in darkness — 1Jo 1:6 — Group 1055). The cluster's characteristics produce transformation in both the irreversible divine and the conditionally maintained human registers.

**[A2 — Human Righteousness]** Mixed in the verse evidence. The Ezekiel stream (A2-002) presents the state as explicitly reversible in both directions — the righteous can turn to wickedness and forfeit, the wicked can turn to righteousness and receive life (Eze 18:21–27; 33:12–19). This is the most explicit statement of reversibility in the cluster. The stability stream (A2-013: "the root of the righteous will never be moved," Pro 12:3) presents a different picture — the righteous person is established and stable. The NT material introduces a new mode: the righteousness conferred through the new birth (1Jo 2:29) and constituted in Christ (2Cor 5:21) is presented as secure — not as perpetually renegotiable. The tension between the Ezekiel reversibility and the NT security is unresolved in the verse evidence alone.

**[C — Justification]** Presented as irreversible in the NT material — the justified person is an heir (Tit 3:7), is freed from condemnation through Christ's intercession (Rom 8:34, VSG 4846-002), stands in a new status before God. Gal 5:4 ("severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace") implies that turning away from the basis of justification does produce a change in standing — suggesting some reversibility in the wrong volitional direction. The irreversibility is secure when the faith-basis is maintained; it is threatened by the abandonment of that basis.

**[G — Structural Opposites]** The hardening of the heart (Rom 2:5, VSG 3207-001) implies increasing irreversibility in the wickedness-direction: the heart becomes progressively harder, suggesting that the capacity for repentance is not indefinitely available. The eschatological crystallisation in Rev 22:11 ("let the evildoer still do evil... let the righteous still do right") presents the final state as irreversible — moral identity is fixed at the eschatological endpoint.

**[CLUSTER]** The verse evidence holds a genuine tension: the OT (Ezekiel) presents moral standing as reversible in both directions; the NT presents the justified standing as secure through Christ's intercession; the eschatological endpoint presents both as irreversible. The tension is not resolved by the verse evidence — it is part of what the programme should document rather than smooth over.
