findings.finding_value: M01-A evidences both reversible and irreversible transformation. The **irreversible** dimension: Jer 32:40 (God implanting the fear as a "permanent inner disposition preventing them from turning away" — permanence is explicit); the "Fear of Isaac" formula (Gen 31:42; 31:53 — anchors A-VCG-06) suggests a defining characterisation that became Isaac's identity, not a reversible episode. The **reversible** dimension: 2Ki 17 corpus (M01-A-VCG-05: the settlers' syncretistic fear shows that genuine fear of God can be corrupted — a reversal of the right inner orientation). Isa 29:13 (fear becoming hollow external formula — a degradation of what was once genuine). The evidence shows transformation can be reversed through corruption, hardened heart (Isa 63:17), and competing allegiance.

M01-B's acute-fear transformations are primarily **reversible** in the moment (fear released when divine reassurance comes: Mat 17:7; Luk 5:10) but can calcify into permanent states (1Sa 18:29: Saul's fear of David intensifies and "becomes permanent — the inner root of his sustained enmity"). Reversibility depends on whether the fear is addressed or left to solidify.

M01-G: 2Ti 1:7 (timidity is not from God) implies it is a reversible condition — the gift of power, love, and self-control is available (2Ti 1:6). But Rev 21:8 (cowardice in the lake of fire) suggests that sustained unchecked timidity culminates in irreversible judgment-state.

The transformation produced by M01 is: reversible in its acute form (M01-B: fear addressed and released); permanently formative in its sustained ordered form (M01-A: Jer 32:40 implantation); reversible through corruption or hardening (M01-A: Isa 29:13; 2Ki 17 corpus); and eschatologically irreversible in its final expression (M01-G: Rev 21:8; M01-A: Rev 11:18 — the redeemed fear God permanently).

For wrath-as-covenantal-verdict: largely irreversible within the historical frame. Heb 3:11 (M02-A-VCG-01) — the oath permanently bars from rest. However, Isa 12:1 (M02-A-VCG-01): "God's anger has turned away" shows that even covenantal wrath can relent when conditions are met — suggesting conditional reversibility.

For burning covenant discipline: reversible through repentance and covenant return. Deu 13:17 (M02-B-VCG-01): burning anger must be "turned from" — turning is possible. Jon 3:9 (M02-B-VCG-01): Ninevites understand that God's burning anger "may be turned aside by repentance." The transformation of national condition (exile) is reversible through the covenant response.

The evidence points to irreversibility for the transformations produced by godly grief. The Corinthians grieved into repentance (2Cor 7:9 — M03-C-VCG-02) — repentance is presented as a lasting change of orientation that "did not bring harm to their souls," not a temporary state. Covenantal distress that turns the will toward God (Deu 4:30; Hos 5:15 — M03-D-VCG-03) is presented as a genuine turning, not a temporary redirection. However, grief itself — as a condition — is presented as reversible: God reverses mourning into dancing (Psa 30:11 — M03-B-VCG-03), and eschatological fullness is the permanent end of grief (Rev 21:4 — M03-B-VCG-04). The grief condition is reversible; the moral transformation it produces tends toward irreversibility.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence shows both. Reversible: the VCG-02 passages (Deu 28:63; Joe 1:16; Isa 16:10; Jer 48:33) show exultation stripped away by judgment — the transformation it produced is reversed when the covenant relationship is broken. Irreversible in eschatological projection: Isa 65:18 commands "be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create" — suggesting the eschatological exultation is permanent, not liable to reversal.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Both registers are evidenced: (1) **Reversible** — Psa 51:8, 12 (David's joy lost and requiring restoration — transformation reversed by sin); Haman's gladness instantly reversed by Mordecai's presence (Est 5:9–14); the rocky-ground joy (Mat 13:20) reversed by testing; the merry-hearted who sigh when the vine fails (Isa 24:7) — circumstantially-grounded joy is reversible; (2) **Irreversible in eschatological form** — Joh 16:22 ("no one will take your joy from you"); Isa 51:11; 35:10 ("everlasting joy" upon the ransomed); Joh 15:11 (fullness of joy as the goal of abiding in Christ); Rev 19:7 (the Lamb's marriage — Joy consummated permanently). Present joy is reversible; eschatological joy is not.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Varies: (1) **Reversible in the fragile form** — M04-F's ba.lag is explicitly temporary and reversible; Job 9:27's attempted cheerfulness fails; Psa 39:13's desired smile is momentary before departure; (2) **Irreversible in the eschatological form** — "no one will take your joy from you" (Joh 16:22 — adjacent) applies to the eschatological form; the "glory to be revealed" (1Pe 4:13) is a permanent eschatological state; (3) **Formation-durable** — the steadfastness produced by Jas 1:3–4 is the durable inner-being deposit of sustained Suffering-Joy; once the person has been formed through trials-in-joy, the proven character is a lasting possession.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Varies by register: (1) **Reversible** — Jon 4:6 (Jonah's gladness in the plant reversed when the plant withers — circumstantially-grounded gladness is reversible); 1Sa 11:9's relief could be reversed by new threats; (2) **Durable** — the ki-tov recognition of divine goodness tends toward durable inner reorientation (the Psalms' sustained praise tradition); (3) **Irreversible in eschatological form** — makarismos (Rom 4:6 — the declared blessedness is a permanent status change before God); Jos 21:45 (not one word has failed — the completeness of fulfilment is irrevocable).

**[CHAR-4]** E — Varies: (1) **Reversible** — Deu 30:9 ("the Lord will again take delight in prospering you") — divine Delight restored after it had been withheld; Eze 18:23; 33:11 (the wicked turning → God's Delight toward life restored) — the divine-Delight relationship is restorable through repentance; (2) **Durable formation** — Psa 1's "tree planted by streams" (from Delight-in-law) images a stable constitutional formation; Psa 119:92's survival of affliction shows durable inner transformation through law-Delight; (3) **Eschatologically permanent** — Isa 62:4 (renamed identity — "My Delight Is in Her") — the eschatological transformation appears permanent; Mal 3:12 ("you will be a land of delight") — the restored state is declared as the permanent eschatological condition; (4) **Corrupt formation** — Isa 66:3's soul-delighting-in-abominations is shown as a deeply entrenched state; whether reversible only through divine intervention is implicit.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Varies: (1) **The ni.cho.ach relationship** — reversible in both directions: Lev 26:31 (God stops receiving aromas — reversible by repentance); Eze 20:41 (God will again accept as pleasing aroma — restoration restoring the Pleasure relationship); (2) **The luxury-curse transformation** (Deu 28:54, 56) — presented as severe but reversible through covenant restoration; (3) **Pro 16:24's health to the body** — implies an ongoing sustaining effect rather than a permanent irreversible change; (4) **Eschatological Pleasure** (Psa 16:11) — "forevermore" implies permanent and irreversible eschatological transformation.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Varies: (1) **Reversible** — Neh 9:17's transformation from wonder to rebellion is reversed by God's mercy (the same verse: "but you are a God ready to forgive, gracious and merciful"); Mic 7:15's "as in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show them marvellous things" shows wonder-based transformation restorable; (2) **Durable** — Psa 71:17's lifelong proclamatory orientation formed by sustained Wonder; (3) **Eschatologically permanent** — Isa 29:14's "wonder upon wonder" pointing toward transformations that the wise cannot reverse; Dan 12:6's end-time wonders producing the permanent transition to the final age.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The comparative pattern reveals a consistent distinction across all seven: **present forms of transformation are reversible; eschatological forms are not**. (1) All seven show reversibility in their present-circumstantial forms: Joy can be lost through sin (Psa 51:8, 12); Delight can be withheld through faithlessness (Mal 1:10); Wonder can fail and produce rebellion (Neh 9:17 — reversed by God's mercy in the same verse); Exultation is stripped by judgment (Joe 1:16); (2) All seven show irreversibility in their eschatological forms: Joy — "no one will take your joy from you" (Joh 16:22); "everlasting joy" (Isa 35:10; 51:11); Delight — "My Delight Is in Her" as permanent identity (Isa 62:4); Pleasure — "pleasures forevermore" (Psa 16:11); Wonder — "wonder upon wonder" as the eschatological escalation (Isa 29:14); Suffering-Joy — unqualified glory-joy at the revelation (1Pe 4:13); (3) **Durable formations** — between reversible and permanent: Delight's formation of the "tree planted by streams" (Psa 1:3) and Suffering-Joy's proven character (Jas 1:3–4) are not permanent in the eschatological sense but are substantially more stable than circumstantially-grounded forms. The cluster's consistent present-reversible/eschatological-permanent pattern confirms its eschatological orientation.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Both conditions are evidenced. The shame of the unjust wound is explicitly declared *reversible* by divine act: Isa 54:4 — "you will forget the shame of your youth"; Isa 61:7 — "instead of your shame there shall be a double portion." The shame of the seared conscience is not declared reversible within the evidence — the passages (Jer 6:15; 8:12) record it as a state of judgment with no restoration promised in context. The transformation shame produces in the corrective mode (2Ch 30:15; Eze 43:10-11) appears stable rather than temporary. The evidence thus shows: unjust shame is reversible by divine promise; appropriate guilt-shame is resolvable through atonement (Eze 16:63); seared-conscience shamelessness is presented as catastrophic and its reversal is not evidenced.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in two trajectories. (1) Corrective transformation: where the humiliated person receives the corrective signal, CHAR-2 produces reorientation of inner standing toward proper proportion. (2) Eschatological transformation: 1Cor 15:43 — the body sown in dishonor is raised in glory — the mortal state of humiliation is explicitly transitional rather than final. David's envoys' humiliation is reversible (2Sa 10:5). VCG-04 evidence (Eze 32; Jer 23:40 — perpetual shame) shows humiliation as permanent in judgment contexts. Reversibility depends on whether divine redemption addresses the humiliation.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 in its active mode produces moral self-contradiction in the dishonorer (Rom 2:23). Heb 6:6 shows apostatic dishonour of Christ as irreversibly damaging — "it is impossible to restore them again to repentance." In the structural mode (VCG-02), 2Ti 2:20 implies that the condition of dishonorable-vessel is tied to moral condition, implying reversibility through moral transformation (cleansing, 2Ti 2:21 context).

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Functioning CHAR-4 produces moral discipline — the renunciation of the shameful and the embrace of transparent, truth-grounded conduct (2Cor 4:2). Inverted CHAR-4 (VCG-03) produces moral deepening of the inversion: "their end is destruction" (Phili 3:19). Rev 16:15's call to vigilance frames CHAR-4's proper functioning as a sustained transformation project oriented toward Christ's coming. Reversibility: the functioning conscience can be restored; the inverted conscience's trajectory ("their end is destruction") is presented as non-reversible in its current direction.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 produces transformation in two directions. (1) Destructive: sustained contempt deposits shame-identity (Bartimaeus's beggar-identity, Mar 10:50). (2) Redemptive: Jesus's reversal of contempt-verdicts (Act 4:11; 1Cor 1:28) transforms the despised into the chosen, overturning the contempt-system's accumulated verdict. The transformation is reversible in both directions: shame-identity can be abandoned (Mar 10:50 — throwing off the cloak); divine reversal can re-assign worth permanently.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 produces the transformation of relational access: from the barrier of guilt-shame to the openness of approach to God. The person with clean hands and a blameless heart (Gen 20:5; Psa 26:6) moves toward God without the inner collapse that guilt-shame would produce. Conversely, the loss of innocence-capacity (Hos 8:5) produces the inverse transformation: from potential access to blocked access. Reversibility: maintained innocence (VCG-01) can be sustained through ongoing moral choices; lost innocence-capacity (Hos 8:5) requires divine intervention for restoration — it is not self-reversible once the capacity has been so deeply damaged.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's transformative patterns fall into four trajectories. (1) Corrective transformation — shame and shamefulness identified as corrective signals that, when received, produce moral reorientation (Chars 1 M07-C, Char 4). Paradigm: 2Ch 30:15 — shame activating priestly consecration; Eze 43:10-11 — Israel's being-ashamed as the precondition for receiving the temple's full design. (2) Eschatological transformation — shame permanently removed and replaced by honour (Char 1's VCG-04 promises); mortal dishonour replaced by resurrection glory (Char 2 — 1Cor 15:43); contempt-verdict overturned by divine vindicating reversal (Char 5 — Act 4:11). (3) Identity transformation — the shame-identity abandoned in response to a higher worth-assignment (Char 5 — Bartimaeus throwing off the cloak; Act 4:11 — the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone). (4) Destructive transformation — the seared conscience, inverted conscience, and loss of innocence-capacity (Chars 1, 4, 6) as transformations in the destructive direction. The cluster's transformative range spans from the most redemptive (eschatological shame-removal) to the most catastrophic (the loss of the conscience's capacity to register moral reality).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Both are evidenced. Reversible: 2Ch 32:26 (vc=34076, M08-A1-VCG-01) — "Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah" — the transformation is reversed through humbling before catastrophic consequence arrives; Dan 4:37 (vc=34094, M08-A4-VCG-04) — Nebuchadnezzar, after being humbled by God's intervention, "praises and extols and honours the King of heaven" — the transformation through CHAR-1 and its subsequent reversal leads to a reoriented inner posture. Irreversible: Isa 14:11 (vc=33988, M08-A3-VCG-02) — "your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers" — the transformation produced by the king of Babylon's pride reaches its terminus in death and total disgrace; Dan 5:20 (vc=34129, M08-A1-VCG-02) — Belshazzar's deposition and loss of glory. The determining factor appears to be whether the person receives divine humbling while reversal is still possible, or whether CHAR-1 is permitted to run to its catastrophic structural end.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence leans strongly toward irreversibility within §3.A. Jer 50:32 (vc=34117, M08-B-VCG-02): "arrogance results in a fall with no one to restore the fallen" — no restoration evidenced. Mal 4:1 (vc=34107, M08-B-VCG-02): "the day that is coming shall set them ablaze... it will leave them neither root nor branch" — total eschatological destruction with no remnant. Neh 9:16/29: the pattern of repeated warnings followed by repeated presumption suggests the transformation CHAR-2 produces is not easily reversed — the Neh 9 historical narrative evidences no sustained reversal within the pattern of presumption. The contrast with CHAR-1's Nebuchadnezzar and Hezekiah reversals is notable: §3.A does not evidence a comparable restoration after CHAR-2. The irreversible end is most prominent.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Both are evidenced, and uniquely to CHAR-3, the transformation can be positive and deliberate. For VCG-01 → VCG-02 transformation: the examination and redirection of the boasting-impulse (Gal 6:14, vc=33869; 2Cor 10:13, vc=33888) is an explicit, sustained transformation that is reversible in principle (the person could revert to VCG-01) but is evidenced as a settled apostolic posture in Paul. For the Pauline examined → God-directed transformation: 1Cor 1:31 (vc=33878, M08-C-VCG-03): "let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord" — commanded as a settled orientation. Unlike CHAR-1 and CHAR-2, CHAR-3 has evidenced positive transformational pathways (VCG-01 → VCG-02 → VCG-03) within the same characteristic.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence leans toward deepening and difficult reversibility. 1Ti 6:4 (vc=33925, M08-D-VCG-02): "understanding nothing" — comprehensive epistemic blindness is a deeply entrenched state; a person who understands nothing cannot easily self-correct since the cognitive faculty that would generate self-correction is the faculty that is impaired. 1Ti 3:6 (vc=33924, M08-D-VCG-02): the condemnation of the devil as the trajectory — judicial finality. No verse in §3.C evidences a restoration or reversal after CHAR-4 has produced its consequences. The counter-mechanisms (love — 1Cor 8:1; sober judgment — Rom 12:3) are preventive rather than curative in the evidence.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Both are evidenced. Irreversible instances: Jer 51:53 (vc=65670, M08-E-VCG-02): even if Babylon fortifies to heaven, "destroyers would come from me against her" — no structural height can prevent God's judgment; Eze 32:12 (vc=33998, M08-E-VCG-01): Egypt's proud might "shall be destroyed" without mention of restoration. Reversible implication: Lev 26:19 (vc=33982, M08-E-VCG-01) is part of the covenant stipulations that include restoration conditions (Lev 26:40–45 — broader covenant context implies restoration is possible after repentance). The evidence leans toward irreversibility in the prophetic-judgment corpus but implies reversibility in the covenantal context.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster comparison reveals a significant asymmetry: CHAR-1 and CHAR-3 evidence reversible pathways (Hezekiah's humbling and reversal in CHAR-1; Nebuchadnezzar's restoration; CHAR-3's VCG-02/03 positive transformation). CHAR-2 and CHAR-5 lean predominantly toward irreversibility (Jer 50:32, M08-B-VCG-02: "fall with no one to restore"; Eze 33:28, M08-E-VCG-01: desolation as the end). CHAR-4's irreversibility is evidenced through the epistemic blindness endpoint ("understanding nothing"). The cluster-synthesis: M08 characteristics are reversible in principle (God can break and restore — Lev 26:19 implies the covenantal restoration possibility; Dan 4:37 evidences Nebuchadnezzar's full restoration after CHAR-1's humbling) but tend toward irreversibility in practice. The determinant of reversibility appears to be whether divine humbling is received before catastrophic collapse or whether CHAR-N is permitted to run to its irreversible terminus.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence suggests the transformation is *conditionally durable*: the sustained character orientation can be disrupted, as 2Th3:14 (the refusal to obey apostolic instruction in those who had previously been part of the community) implies. However, the soul-purification of 1Pe1:22 and the identity-formation of 1Pe1:14 suggest deep transformations that are not easily reversed. Phile21 — Paul's confidence in Philemon's obedience as a reliable disposition — implies a durability that characterises genuine formation rather than superficial compliance. The obedience that is "always obeyed" (Phili2:12) and "even more in my absence" suggests a durability that has become characterological rather than situational.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The two-verse corpus does not directly address reversibility. The reviving of spirit and heart (Isa57:15) implies a restoration that God actively sustains. However, since contrition can in principle recur (the characteristic is the acute response to moral failure, and persons can fail again), the transformation is not simply once-for-all — it may be entered repeatedly. The characteristic appears to be *durably formative* in the orientation it establishes (opening toward God rather than self-asserting) while being episodically renewable as an acute state.

**[CHAR-4]** S — The two-verse corpus does not directly address the reversibility of transformation produced by this characteristic. The evidence describes the characteristic as a capacity and quality rather than addressing its long-term transformative effects.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The three-verse corpus does not directly address the reversibility of the transformations produced by semnotēs. The characteristic's relational-ordering effects persist while the characteristic is genuinely present and can be lost if the inner character quality is not maintained.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The transformation is *reversible* — Psa51:12 directly evidences this. The willing spirit that was once present was lost through moral failure (the prayer would be unnecessary if the transformation were irreversible). The characteristic can be lost and restored — the transformation is thus conditional and reversible by the person's moral choices and by God's restorative grace. This makes willing-heartedness distinctively fragile compared to some other inner-being characteristics: it requires both genuine inner freedom and divine sustaining to persist.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence suggests the transformation is *conditionally reversible* in the covenantal condition dimension, but *characterologically durable* in the orientation dimension. 2Ch33:23 — Amon did not humble himself as Manasseh his father had — implying Manasseh's transformation was not automatically transmitted and the characteristic's effects do not automatically persist across persons or generations. However, the character-garment language of Col3:12 ("put on… humility") implies a transformation that, once genuinely established as a worn disposition, is durable in the person's character. Phili4:12 ("I have *learned*") — the learning verb implies an acquired and retained capacity. The evidence distinguishes the eventive covenantal condition change (which can be lost by subsequent unfaithfulness) from the characterological orientation change (which is durably acquired when genuine).

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster contains both, and the contrast is theologically significant. *Most explicitly reversible*: CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness — Psa51:12 directly evidences that the willing spirit can be lost through moral failure and must be sought again. CHAR-1 Humility in the covenantal-condition register: 2Ch33:23 (Amon's failure to humble as Manasseh had) suggests the transformation is not automatically transmitted. *Most conditionally durable*: CHAR-2 Submission — soul-purification (1Pe1:22) and identity-formation (1Pe1:14) suggest deep transformations, though 2Th3:14 evidences possible relapse. *Character-level transformations* (CHAR-4, CHAR-5): the capacity for metriopatheō and the quality of semnotēs are characterological and thus more stable, though not invulnerable to character-loss. Cluster-level: CHAR-6's explicit reversibility is unique in the cluster — it is the only characteristic whose corpus contains a direct narrative of the characteristic being lost and sought again (Psa51:12). This makes willing-heartedness M09's most fragile characteristic and the most clearly dependent on divine sustaining. The cluster's most stable transformation (CHAR-2 identity-level soul-purification) contrasts with its most fragile (CHAR-6 willing spirit subject to moral failure).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — The transformation is primarily evidenced as reversible through divine action. 2Sa 12:13 — Nathan declares: "The Lord also has put away your sin; you shall not die." The condition change (guilt → forgiven) is reversed by God's act of putting away. 1Ki 8:33/35 — Solomon's prayer structure presupposes reversibility: if the people "turn again to you and acknowledge your name and pray," God will forgive (1Ki 8:50). The cultic-atonement corpus (VCG-04: Lev 4:35/5:10/5:13 — "and he shall be forgiven") shows that the condition change from sinning is reversed through the prescribed remedy. Eze 3:21 confirms reversibility at the orientation level: the righteous person warned not to sin "does not sin" — the trajectory can be held or altered. However, the escalation pattern (Hos 4:7/13:2) suggests that sustained sinning without reversal progressively narrows the window for reversal — not closing it by divine decree, but by the hardening of the inner person.

**[CHAR-10]** E — Variable across mechanisms. (1) *Enticement*: the transformation evidenced in 2Pe 2:14 is severe ("hearts trained" — the perfect participle implies completed formation) but the broader 2Pe 2 context presents the false teachers as heading toward judgment rather than as irreversibly beyond restoration. The "barely escaping" recipients of 2Pe 2:18 — the enticement has not yet fully captured them, implying the possibility of reversal before capture is complete. (2) *Hypocrisy*: Gal 2:13 — Paul's confrontation of Peter implies the reversal is possible: the hypocrisy is being publicly named and called out, suggesting it is addressable. (3) *Apostasy*: Act 21:21 — the accusation context implies the apostasy is perceived as reversible (the community seeks to correct the perceived teaching). Within this corpus, no mechanism is presented as producing an irreversible transformation.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Conditionally reversible with one absolute irreversible exception. (1) *Generally reversible*: VCG-02's entire 39-verse register evidences that the condition's debt-dimension is reversible: "your sins are forgiven" (Mat 9:2); "blotted out" (Act 3:19); "take away their sins" (Rom 11:27). The condition can be addressed through Christ's atoning work and faith-repentance response. (2) *Irreversible exception*: Mat 12:31 — "the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven" — this specific form of engagement with the condition crosses a threshold that forgiveness cannot reach. (3) *Ultimate eschatological irreversibility*: Joh 8:21/24 — "you will die in your sins" — for those who remain in the condition without receiving the remedy, the final death in the condition is eschatologically irreversible; the condition's ultimate consequence (eternal separation from where Jesus goes) is final.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Conditionally reversible with one irreversible exception. (1) *Generally reversible through new birth*: 1Jo 3:9 — the new-birth transformation reverses the enslaving power's hold; the formerly enslaved person "cannot keep on sinning" — the slavery's constitutional grip is reversed. (2) *Irreversible exception — sin leading to death*: 1Jo 5:16 — "there is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that" — this form of enslavement produces a trajectory toward death that the intercessory remedy cannot reach; the enslaving power in its most severe form generates an irreversible transformation. (3) *Rom 6:2 posture confirms reversibility for believers*: "how can we who died to sin still live in it?" — the death-to-sin that believers have undergone is a completed transformation that reverses the prior enslaved state.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Generally reversible through divine action, with one irreversible dimension. (1) *Reversible*: Eze 33:16 — "none of the sins that he has committed shall be remembered against him" — the record's account-against-the-person is reversible through repentance and divine erasure; Isa 43:25 — God blots out the record as a sovereign act; Jer 31:34 — the new covenant promises permanent erasure; (2) *Irreversible dimension*: Jer 17:1 — "engraved on the tablet of their heart" — the internal heart-engraving of the sin-pattern is presented as indelible without divine intervention (the iron pen, diamond point imagery); (3) *Neh 4:5 — the enemies' sins called not to be blotted out* — this prayer for irreversible judgment implies a state where the record can be fixed for reckoning, though the general pattern is erasability through divine action.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Provisional (OT register)*: VCG-01 — kip.pu.rim operates "once in the year throughout your generations" (Exo 30:10) — the annual cycle implies the covering is temporary and must be renewed; the OT transformation is real but provisional; (2) *Permanent (NT register)*: Col 1:14 — "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" — present tense, permanent possession; Eph 1:7 — "in him we have redemption through his blood" — the blood-atonement produces a permanent transformation; (3) *Irreversibly foreclosed*: Mar 3:29 — "is guilty of an eternal sin" — the eternal-sin condition produces a permanent un-transformation (permanent unforgiveness); the inverse of the characteristic's positive transformation is also permanent.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Reversible through divine intervention and human heart-turning. 1Ki 8:47 — "if they turn their heart... and repent and plead with you" — the conditional structure indicates reversibility: the turning is possible even within the long-duration condition; Eze 37:23 — "I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them" — God's sovereign cleansing reverses what the accumulated sinning produced. The condition is not irremovable but requires the specific combination of volitional turning (human side) and divine cleansing (divine side) to reverse.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Reversible — with one exception. Psa 51:13 — "sinners will return to you" — the return implies the sinner-identity's reversibility; Luk 15:7/10 — the repentant sinner generates cosmic joy, confirming the reversal is real; 1Ti 1:15/16 — Paul as foremost sinner transformed to apostle is the paradigmatic reversal. The single irreversible direction: Psa 104:35 — "let sinners be consumed from the earth" — the eschatological consumption is final; Isa 13:9 — sinners destroyed on the day of the Lord — the judgment-transformation is irreversible once enacted. The reversal through repentance is possible before judgment; the judgment-transformation is irreversible after it.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Reversible — through divine action*: Isa 6:7 — guilt taken away; Jer 33:8 — cleansed from all guilt; Psa 34:22 — not condemned when taking refuge; (2) *Progressive accumulation toward irreversibility*: 2Ch 33:23 — "incurred guilt more and more" — the progressive accumulation moves the condition toward greater difficulty of reversal; Jer 2:22 — the indelible stain that lye cannot remove suggests a depth of guilt that self-effort cannot reverse; (3) *Eschatological irreversibility*: Eze 21:25 — "the time of your final punishment" — once judgment arrives at the appointed final time, the guilt's consequential transformation is irreversible.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Reversible through divine action*: Jer 50:20 — "iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none" — the iniquity record is entirely erasable; Zec 3:9 — "I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day"; Mic 7:19 — "he will tread our iniquities underfoot"; (2) *Eschatologically irreversible for some*: Isa 22:14 — "surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die" — within the person's lifetime, no reversal; 1Sa 3:14 — "the iniquity of Eli's house shall not be atoned for by sacrifice or offering forever" — beyond sacrifice; (3) *Progressively deepening without address*: 2Ch 33:23 (cross-ref) — "incurred guilt more and more" — the accumulation without address deepens toward irreversibility.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Reversible through repentance and divine pardon*: Eze 18:28 — turning reverses the death-sentence; Psa 103:12 — "as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us" — fully reversible through divine act; Isa 44:22 — "I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud" — total erasure; (2) *Irreversible for persistent rebels*: Isa 66:24 — "their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched" — the end of persistent rebellion is permanent, irrevocable judgment; Exo 23:21 — "he will not pardon your transgression" — in specific contexts non-pardon is declared irrevocable; (3) *Conditionally limited*: Amos 1:3 — "I will not revoke the punishment" — once the threshold is reached, reversal of judgment is foreclosed even if individual repentance remains possible.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The condition transformation is reversible through the prescribed remedy. Lev 4:2 (sin incurred) → Num 15:27 (offering brought) → Num 15:28 ("he shall be forgiven") — the full sequence is explicitly reversible: the liability created by inadvertent sinning is addressed and closed by the atonement mechanism. Lev 19:22 — "he shall be forgiven for the sin that he has committed" — the forgiveness declaration closes the liability condition. The reversibility is built into the system: the Levitical provision for unintentional sinning is precisely a prescribed reversal mechanism. No irreversible trajectory is evidenced in the CHAR-2 corpus for the personal-moral register (VCG-01).

**[CHAR-20]** E — Primarily reversible through covenant-confession, with exceptions. (1) *Reversible through confession*: Lev 26:40-42 — "if they confess their iniquity and... treachery... I will remember my covenant" — the covenant-memory restoration reverses the transformation; (2) *Individual irreversible case*: 1Ch 10:13 — "Saul died for his breach of faith" — the death-verdict is irreversible for Saul individually; the faithlessness that produced his death cannot be reversed posthumously; (3) *Progressive deepening toward irreversibility*: 2Ch 28:22 — Ahaz becoming "yet more faithless" — the progressive deepening suggests a trajectory toward irreversibility, but the corpus does not explicitly name Ahaz's faithlessness as beyond recovery.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Reversible through renewal*: Eph 4:23 — "renewed in the spirit of your minds"; 2Pe 1:4 — escape into divine nature; Gal 6:8 — Spirit-sowing producing eternal life; (2) *Eschatologically final for the unrepentant*: Rev 19:2 — Babylon judged and destroyed; 1Cor 3:17 — "God will destroy him" who destroys the temple; 2Pe 2:12 — "destroyed in their destruction" — the animal-instinctual corruption reaches its eschatological irreversible endpoint; (3) *Progressive deepening without address*: Eph 4:22 — "corrupt through deceitful desires" — the ongoing-tense verb (*phtheiromenos* — is being corrupted) indicates a progressive process that deepens without the intervention of the putting-off/putting-on.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Both dimensions evidenced. (1) *Reversible through cessation and restitution*: Eze 33:15 — the wicked who stops doing injustice and restores pledges "shall surely live"; Job 34:32 — "I will do it no more" — volitional reversibility; (2) *Eschatologically finalised for the persistent unjust*: 1Cor 6:9 — "the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God" — the final eschatological irreversibility for the character-level unjust; 2Pe 2:9 — "keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment" — sustained divine custody awaiting final judgment; (3) *Character-level resistance*: Luk 16:10 — "dishonest in very little is also dishonest in much" — the fixed character-scale suggests deep constitutional resistance to reversal, though Eze 33:15 keeps the path open.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The condition-transformation (sin-record cancelled — Eze 33:16) is presented as effective and complete when genuine. The orientation-transformation is evidenced as sustainable when the confession is genuine (Luk 15:21 — the prodigal's confession initiates a restored relationship that the narrative does not reverse) and unsustained when hollow (Exo 9:27/10:16 — Pharaoh's confessions are reversed when the plagues cease: the orientation returns to hardness). The reversibility thus tracks the genuineness of the confession: genuine confession produces orientation-change that is sustained; hollow confession produces apparent orientation-change that reverts under pressure.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The corpus presents conscience suppression as *reversible* in principle, though increasingly difficult to reverse with habituation. 1Cor 15:34 — "wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning" — the imperative "wake up" presupposes that awakening is possible: the stupor is not permanent. The call to shame ("I say this to your shame") implies that the shame-response can still be activated — the conscience has not been permanently destroyed. However, Tit 3:11's "warped" (*exestraptai* — perfect participle: completed deformation) suggests that advanced conscience suppression produces a constitutional state that is harder to reverse: the person is already deformed. The corpus does not evidence any state of irreversible conscience suppression, but the trajectory of Tit 3:11 suggests deepening difficulty.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The corpus presents a spectrum. (1) *Reversible in principle throughout most of the corpus*: the Kings pattern implies reversibility — each king who "did not depart from" could have departed; God's warnings (Neh 9:29 — "to turn them back") presuppose that turning was possible. Eze 33:12 — "the wickedness of the wicked, he shall not fall by it when he *turns from* his wickedness" — turning is presented as always remaining available, reversing the condition. (2) *Foreclosed at the Heb 10:26 threshold*: "there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins" — at the point of deliberate sinning after knowledge of truth, the reversal mechanism (sacrifice) is described as closed. The corpus thus presents: reversible across most of the trajectory of refusal, but reaching a point of irreversibility at the extreme end (Heb 10:26).

**[CHAR-6]** E — The corpus presents the transformation as *potentially reversible in principle but practically resistant*. 1Ki 8:46 — Solomon's prayer envisions a path of restoration for those who have sinned and been taken captive: hearing, repenting, returning — the reversibility is built into the prayer's structure. 1Jo 3:6 — "no one who abides in him keeps on sinning" — the abiding relationship structurally prevents and (by implication) reverses the habitual pattern. However, the practical difficulty of reversal is implied by Exo 9:34's hardening cycle (the hardening makes each subsequent reversal harder), Heb 3:17's terminal consequence for the wilderness generation (bodies fell — for them, no reversal), and 1Sa 2:25's "it was the will of the Lord to put them to death" — at the extreme end, the reversal is no longer available.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The corpus presents the transformation as *reversible in principle but requiring structural dismantling*. 2Ki 23:15 — Josiah's demolition of Jeroboam's altar — is the evidence of reversibility: the physical structure through which the contagious sin was being perpetuated is removed. However, Josiah's demolition occurs approximately three centuries after Jeroboam's contagious sin transmission began, suggesting the reversal is extremely difficult and long-delayed. 1Ki 14:16 — "he will give Israel up" — at the extreme end, the condition-change produced by sustained contagious sin across generations is effectively irreversible (Israel is exiled). The practical trajectory is toward irreversibility with sustained transmission; reversal is structurally possible but historically exceptional (Josiah) and increasingly difficult with time.

**[CHAR-8]** E — The corpus presents the transformation as *effectively irreversible within the historical horizon*. All four "to this day" markers (1Ki 12:19; 2Ki 8:22; 2Ch 10:19; 2Ch 21:10) name permanently enduring revolts: the political fracture remains to the narrator's present without restoration. No verse in the corpus describes a reversal of the political revolt — no returning to submission, no restoration of the broken governing relationship. The transformation is presented as effectively permanent within the timeframe the corpus addresses.

**[CHAR-9]** E — The corpus presents a spectrum. (1) *Irreversible*: Mat 12:31 — "will not be forgiven" — the Spirit-blasphemy form produces permanent irreversible transformation. (2) *Reversible*: 1Ti 1:13 — Paul's blasphemy was reversed by mercy; Mar 3:28 — "all sins will be forgiven... and whatever blasphemies they utter" — the general category of sinful speech is forgivable. Eph 4:31 / Col 3:8 — the commands to put away slander presuppose that the transformation of the slanderous disposition is achievable. The reversibility thus depends entirely on the form: most sinful speech is forgivable; Spirit-blasphemy is not.

**[CHAR-1]** E — The evidence presents both reversible and irreversible trajectories. The reversible trajectory is documented through the Ezekiel repentance corpus (VCG-07): Eze 18:21-22 — "if a wicked person turns away from all his sins… he shall surely live, he shall not die"; Eze 33:14-16 — the death-sentence is lifted when the wicked turns. The reversal is volitional, concrete (restitution acts — Eze 33:15), and effective (life results — Eze 33:19). The irreversible trajectory appears in: Isa 26:10 (VCG-05 — the wicked who cannot learn righteousness even under grace); Dan 12:10 (VCG-05 — "none of the wicked shall understand" — eschatological hardening); Pro 5:22 (VCG-06 — the bondage of the wicked's own cords). The evidence does not present a fixed point at which reversibility becomes definitively impossible, but the eschatological texts (Dan 12:10; Psa 9:5; Mal 4:3) imply a final termination after which reversal is no longer in view.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence presents transformation as reversible in principle, through divine action. Act 3:26 (vc=14410 — VCG-05): "to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness" — divine blessing produces the turn from the constitutional evil; the characteristic is not permanently fixed. Heb 10:22 (vc=14426 — VCG-06): the evil conscience can be "sprinkled clean" — this is a real transformation of the constitutional condition. Tit 3:3 (vc=14367 — VCG-05) describes a "former" state of malice and envy now replaced — the transformation is evidenced as historically accomplished in the community being addressed. However, 2Ti 3:13 (vc=14451 — VCG-06) shows the trajectory without divine intervention: "from bad to worse" — the characteristic moves toward increasing irreversibility. The pattern is: reversible through divine transformative action; self-reinforcing toward increasing irreversibility without it.

**[CHAR-3]** E — The evidence presents transformation as reversible in principle through divine action. Eze 14:6 (vc=65984 — VCG-04) explicitly calls for turning from abominations — the reversal is commanded, implying it is possible. Eze 36:31 (vc=1681 — VCG-04): divine action restores memory, which produces self-loathing and conscience-reawakening — the transformation of the silenced conscience is reversible through divine initiative. The sustained silencing of conscience (Jer 6:15; 8:12 — VCG-04) represents the trajectory toward irreversibility — not an achieved permanent state but a deepening hardening. Rev 21:27 (vc=22 — VCG-05) and Eze 44:13 (vc=66003 — VCG-04) name eschatological-terminal consequences (permanent exclusion, permanent shame-bearing) that imply a final irreversibility at the eschatological horizon. The pattern is: reversible through divine action in the present; trajectory toward irreversibility without such action; eschatological finality at the terminus.

**[CHAR-4]** E — The evidence presents the transformation as reversible through divine action. Eze 37:23 (vc=65913 — VCG-05): "I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them" — divine reversal of the characteristic's transformation. 2Ch 34:33 (vc=65946 — VCG-03): Josiah's removal of all abominations enabled sustained devotion — the communal transformation is reversible through reform. Jer 4:1 (vc=65903 — VCG-04): "If you return… If you remove your detestable things from my presence" — the condition for reversal is stated as achievable. The trajectory without divine intervention is toward irreversibility: Jer 44:22 (vc=65967 — VCG-04): the Lord "could no longer bear" — suggesting a threshold beyond which judgment rather than restoration becomes the primary trajectory. Reversible through divine action; moving toward irreversibility without it.

**[CHAR-5]** E — The evidence presents the transformation as reversible through divine action and human volitional response. Isa 55:7 (vc=38200 — VCG-02): "let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, that he may have compassion on him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon" — reversal is both commanded and promised as achievable. Job 36:10 (vc=38215 — VCG-04): "He opens their ears to instruction and commands that they return from iniquity" — divine action enables reversal. Jer 4:14 (vc=38205 — VCG-02): "wash your heart from evil, that you may be saved" — the commanded washing implies reversibility. However, the terminus of the sustained trajectory (Psa 36:12 — vc=38233 — VCG-04: "evildoers lie fallen; they are thrust down, unable to rise") and Psa 92:7 (VCG-03: "doomed to destruction forever") describe a point of irrecoverability — irreversibility at the eschatological terminus of the trajectory without intervention.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The VCG-01 evidence presents the hardened-blasphemy trajectory as moving toward irreversibility. Rev 16:9/11/21 (VCG-01): three successive escalating judgments produce no repentance — the reversibility becomes progressively less available as each judgment deepens the hardening. The Revelation context (eschatological judgment) implies a final terminus: the plagues are the last judgments; if they produce no repentance, the trajectory is terminally fixed. However, for VCG-03: 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): some false accusers "may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation" — partial reversibility is possible for at least some false accusers; their false speech is not permanently fixed. The distinction is between VCG-01's eschatological hardened trajectory (effectively irreversible at that terminus) and VCG-02/03's more reversible social-false-speech.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's unanimous pattern: transformation is reversible through divine action prior to the eschatological terminus, with the trajectory moving toward irreversibility without such action. All six characteristics evidence reversibility: Char 1 (Eze 18:21-27 — turning from wickedness), Char 2 (Act 3:26 — divine transformation), Char 3 (Eze 36:31 — memory-restoration enabling return), Char 4 (Eze 37:23 — divine cleansing), Char 5 (Isa 55:7 — forsake thoughts and return), Char 6 (the implied repentance option of Rev 16:9 that is not taken). The irreversibility threshold: all six characteristics also show a trajectory toward a point of no return — Char 6 most explicitly (the eschatological blasphemers of Rev 16 who do not repent across three successive judgments), Chars 1 and 2 through the eschatological-separation evidence (Mat 13:49; Psa 36:12). The cluster's temporal structure: reversible at any point prior to the eschatological terminus; effectively irreversible at the terminus.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Primarily reversible. The standard defilement pattern — "shall be unclean until the evening; then it shall be clean" (Lev 11:24 and throughout M10c-A-VCG-02, -05, -06) — is structurally reversible. The corpse-contact defilement (seven-day, M10c-A-VCG-07) is more severe but still resolved through the prescribed remedy (Num 19:19-20). However, irreversible sub-cases exist: (1) earthenware vessels that must be broken (Lev 11:33, M10c-A-VCG-03) — irreversible for that object; (2) condemned diseased house demolished (Lev 14:44-45, M10c-B-VCG-04) — irreversible for that structure; (3) willful non-cleansing resulting in excision from the assembly (Num 19:20, M10c-A-VCG-07) — the social consequence is irreversible in that moment. The reversibility pattern applies to persons; the irreversibility applies to certain objects and to the social consequence of willful non-remedy.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Primarily reversible within the 26-verse corpus's frame. The call to cleansing (2Cor 7:1, VCG-03) and separation (2Cor 6:17, VCG-03) presupposes reversibility — the imperative only makes sense if the condition can be changed. 1Th 4:7 (VCG-02) — "God has not called us for impurity, but in holiness" — the divine calling toward holiness implies the person can respond and be transformed. The threat of unrepentance at 2Cor 12:21 (VCG-02) — Paul fears those who "have not repented" — shows that repentance remains available; the condition is not named as irreversible. The Eph 5:5 (VCG-04) exclusion from inheritance is a warning about the current state, not a declaration of permanent irreversibility. The characteristic is serious and escalating, but within the 26-verse corpus it is not framed as permanently irreversible.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Primarily reversible at the eschatological level, though some specific consequences are irreversible within the historical frame. Reversible: Eze 37:23 (VCG-05) — "they shall not defile themselves anymore... and will cleanse them" — divine cleansing reverses the condition; Zec 13:1 (VCG-05) — the fountain of cleansing. Historically irreversible consequences: the destruction of the temple (Psa 79:1, VCG-03), the desecration of idolatrous altars by Josiah (2Ki 23, VCG-02 — these sites are deliberately permanently desecrated), the exile as a historical event. However, the exilic condition itself is treated as reversible through restoration: Isa 52:1 (VCG-05) — the holy city will no longer admit the unclean. The defilement is reversible at the deepest level through divine cleansing, even where specific historical consequences cannot be undone.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Fully reversible through divine authority. Luk 6:18 — "were cured"; Act 5:16 — "were all healed" — complete restoration implies reversibility. Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 (VCG-02) — the spirit seeks re-entry after expulsion — potential vulnerability to re-possession noted, but this is a dynamic of spiritual vulnerability rather than irreversibility of the initial restoration. Mar 9:25 (VCG-01): "never enter him again" — the command against re-entry explicitly addresses the reversibility concern.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's reversibility profile reveals a nuanced picture. All four characteristics are primarily reversible — all have prescribed or evidenced restoration pathways. Characteristic 1: reversible through prescribed remedy (washing, waiting, water of impurity), with limited irreversibility for objects (broken earthenware — Lev 11:33) and the social consequence of willful non-remedy (Num 19:20 — excision). Characteristic 2: reversible — the call to cleansing (2Cor 7:1) and the divine calling toward holiness (1Th 4:7) presuppose reversibility; the characteristic is serious but not named as permanently irreversible. Characteristic 3: reversible at the eschatological level through divine cleansing (Eze 37:23 — "will cleanse them"; Zec 13:1 — fountain of cleansing) even where specific historical consequences (temple destruction, exile) cannot be undone within history. Characteristic 4: fully reversible through divine authority (Luk 6:18 — "cured"; Act 5:16 — "all healed"; Mar 9:25 — "never enter him again"). The cluster's unanimous reversibility finding: every register of defilement is reversible — none is named as beyond divine cleansing. This is the cluster's most important eschatological finding: the M10c domain is a domain of conditions that God can and does reverse. The design of the M10c cluster is toward restoration, not toward permanent defilement.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-005: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's stan…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's standing AND orientation-change in his reception of identity). Second, the formative cycle is self-reinforcing: the after-state of compassion-received feeds back into the before-state of compassion-readiness in the future — the person who has received compassion becomes more capable of extending it. Third, compassion plays a dual role in the sanctification arc: it is simultaneously the character target being formed (the person becoming compassionate over time) and the motivational ground that makes the formative relationship survivable through failure and return. Matthew 18:27 introduces the most critical formative warning: received compassion can be forfeited by failure to extend it — compassion is not a permanently possessed gift but a participatory moral framework. Three distinct mechanisms of change operate across contexts: encounter/sudden (splanchnizō — the moment of being moved), covenantal-sustaining/gradual (chesed — the steady faithfulness over time), and participatory-ontological (2Pe 1:4 pattern — sharing in what God is). T5.7 is formally closed: no body deposit established. All four relationships between suffering and compassion are evidenced — suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-011: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation pr…
findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect analysis (largely P-rated because the receiver's inner-being experience is absent) and T5's formation arc together reveal a gap that is structurally significant: the formation process from single compassion-event to compassion-character is the most important untraced developmental relationship in the registry. T5 provides the directional finding (the formative cycle feeds back from after-state to before-state) and names the three mechanisms (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological). T1 provides the definitional starting point (compassion as character quality is the endpoint of formation). Together they frame an arc that is identified but not filled: how does the moment of splanchnizō (T1 inner-event) accumulate into the settled character of ra.chum (T1 character quality)? T5's mechanisms suggest the answer but the data does not trace the path explicitly — a gap confirmed by both tiers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-016: T2's four-stage constitutional movement (somatic arousal → soul → volition → action) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) ar…
findings.finding_value: T2's four-stage constitutional movement (somatic arousal → soul → volition → action) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally complementary. T2 describes the movement within a single compassion-event; T5 describes how that event accumulates into character over time. The encounter/sudden mechanism (T5) corresponds to the full four-stage sequence of T2 in a single instance. The covenantal-sustaining mechanism (T5) corresponds to the repeated operation of the somatic-soul pathway (T2.2 — soul-level chesed as the sustaining character) over time. The participatory-ontological mechanism (T5) corresponds to the constitutional direction T2 identifies but leaves at spirit-level gap: if the deepest formation is participatory-ontological, the spirit-level dimension (T2.1 — entirely silent) may be where this operates — a convergent gap from two tiers.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-020: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connecte…
findings.finding_value: T3's affect-moral-action unity (affect is the mechanism, not the precursor) and T5's formation finding (compassion is simultaneously character target and motivational ground) are structurally connected. T5 names compassion as the motivational ground that makes the sanctification arc survivable through failure and return — but T3 has already established that affect is the mechanism of this motivational ground: the character formation that T5 describes is accomplished through the affective mechanism that T3 identifies. The person who is formed into compassionate character (T5) is the person whose affective faculty has been trained to respond immediately and morally to perceived suffering (T3). T3's finding that affect and moral action are unified is T5's mechanism of formation: the person becoming compassionate is the person in whom the affective-moral unity is deepening and stabilising.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-023-023: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, cove…
findings.finding_value: T4's finding that divine compassion operates on three simultaneous bases (sovereignly free, covenantally grounded, situationally responsive) and T5's three mechanisms of change (encounter/sudden, covenantal-sustaining/gradual, participatory-ontological) are structurally isomorphic. The sovereignly-free basis corresponds to the encounter/sudden mechanism: divine compassion operating freely produces the sudden compassion-event (splanchnizō). The covenantally-grounded basis corresponds to the covenantal-sustaining mechanism: chesed as the sustaining relational ground operates gradually and consistently. The situationally-responsive basis opens toward the participatory-ontological mechanism: formation at the deepest constitutional level produces a person who is dispositionally responsive to every situation of need. findings.finding_value: T5's three mechanisms of change explain the structural pattern visible in T6's co-occurrence landscape. The encounter/sudden mechanism (splanchnizō producing immediate transformation) corresponds to the high co-occurrence with despair (28 verses) and distress (16 verses) — these are the conditions that trigger the sudden compassion-event. The covenantal-sustaining mechanism corresponds to the high co-occurrence with love (196 verses), mercy (76 verses), and covenant (17 verses) — these are the characteristics that share the sustaining, gradual register with chesed. The participatory-ontological mechanism corresponds to the sequential relationship (compassion → mercy confirmed as constitutionally causal in T6.2) — the deepest formation mechanism produces the person who naturally extends mercy as the externalised form of the compassion-character formed within. Formation mechanisms (T5) explain co-occurrence patterns (T6).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-005: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outp…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outpouring (Zec 12:10), word (Act 20:32 — grace operating through the proclaimed word), inference (Rom 8:32 — cognitive reasoning from the supreme grace-event to present assurance), and mediated-transformation (grace → tenderheartedness → forgiving — Eph 4:32, SD030). Five distinct mechanisms for a single characteristic is unique in the programme data. The creaturely recognition response (fear → mourning → prostration) is confirmed as a consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences across different evidential contexts — not incidental detail but structural feature. Suffering's relationship to grace is precisely distinguished: grace inhabits suffering rather than suffering producing grace (2Cor 12:9 — weakness as theatre of grace, not as generator of grace). The reversibility question (T5.1 P2) is the most significant gap: not fully resolved. The eschatological trajectory (T5.6) is evidenced through Eph 2:7 ("the immeasurable riches of his grace in the coming ages") and charitoō's perfect-passive form (completed state with continuing effect). T2.8 remains open; T5.7 is formally left open accordingly.

findings.finding_value: T1's sustained-effect finding (immediate/sustained contrast as qualitative, not merely temporal — what grace does immediately is creaturely recognition; what it does over time is constitution of identity and character) maps onto T5's formation mechanisms. The encounter mechanism (T5) produces the immediate effects named in T1.5; the word, inference, and mediated-transformation mechanisms (T5) produce the sustained effects of T1.6. T5's five mechanisms collectively explain how the four kinds named in T1.2 are produced across different temporal and contextual registers: disposition-receipt is the encounter mechanism; standing is the spirit-outpouring mechanism; capacity is the mediated-transformation mechanism; character quality is the sustained word-and-inference mechanism. T1 names what is produced; T5 names how each kind is produced.

findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (SD021 sequence: disposition → standing → capacity → character) and T5's five formation mechanisms describe the same formation arc from spatial and temporal perspectives. T2 identifies the constitutional levels through which grace moves; T5 identifies the mechanisms by which grace moves through each level in different contexts. The encounter mechanism (T5 — sudden specific relational event) produces the spirit-level reception (T2.1 — the initial point of arrival). The word mechanism (T5 — Act 20:32 — grace through proclaimed word) produces the soul-standing establishment (T2.2 — the word's sustained effect on the person's constitutive condition). The mediated-transformation mechanism (T5 — tenderheartedness → forgiving — Eph 4:32, SD030) corresponds to T2.7's bidirectional body-soul finding: the inner transformation mediates outward through the body-soul interface. T2.8's open question (body deposit) and T5.7's open status are formally aligned — both pending further investigation.

findings.finding_value: T3's faculty findings are the synchronic expression of T5's diachronic formation arc. The creaturely recognition response (T5.2 — fear → mourning → prostration as the consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences) is the affective-faculty event (T3.4) at the moment of grace-arrival, which then constitutes the volitional-faculty alignment (T3.6 — the agency-constituting paradox) that enables the conscientious expression (T3.10). T5's formation arc (sustained work producing character-quality) is the longitudinal development of T3.9's finding (conscience operating fully within grace) into T3.10's finding (conscientiousness as the integrated moral character that grace constitutes over time). The person who has been formed by grace through the T5 formation arc is the person in whom T3's faculty engagements have been progressively deepened and integrated.

findings.finding_value: T5's most distinctive formation finding (five mechanisms, creaturely recognition response as consistent transitional state, grace inhabiting rather than resolving suffering) is grounded in and confirmed by T7's vocabulary and textual evidence. The NT coinage charitoō (T7.1 P9 — coined for standing-in-favour as completed, continuing state) is the lexical ground of T5.1's irreversibility finding: the perfect passive grammatical form encodes precisely the "transformation not reversed" character that T5.1 identifies. T7.2's argument structure analysis (Zec 12:10 — grace outpoured → recognition → mourning → supplication) is the textual grounding for T5.2's creaturely recognition response finding: the sequence is not an incidental narrative feature but an argued structural pattern. T7.3's framework divergence (human science frameworks assuming prior capacity; Scripture denying it at the point of maximum incapacity — Eph 2:1-5) is the methodological expression of T5.5's deepest formation finding: the person cannot initiate their own formation by grace. T5 and T7 describe the same formation reality from narrative and lexical angles.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, in two trajectories. (1) Corrective transformation: where the humiliated person receives the corrective signal, CHAR-2 produces reorientation of inner standing toward proper proportion. (2) Eschatological transformation: 1Cor 15:43 — the body sown in dishonor is raised in glory — the mortal state of humiliation is explicitly transitional rather than final. David's envoys' humiliation is reversible (2Sa 10:5). VCG-04 evidence (Eze 32; Jer 23:40 — perpetual shame) shows humiliation as permanent in judgment contexts. Reversibility depends on whether divine redemption addresses the humiliation.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — CHAR-3 in its active mode produces moral self-contradiction in the dishonorer (Rom 2:23). Heb 6:6 shows apostatic dishonour of Christ as irreversibly damaging — "it is impossible to restore them again to repentance." In the structural mode (VCG-02), 2Ti 2:20 implies that the condition of dishonorable-vessel is tied to moral condition, implying reversibility through moral transformation (cleansing, 2Ti 2:21 context).

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Functioning CHAR-4 produces moral discipline — the renunciation of the shameful and the embrace of transparent, truth-grounded conduct (2Cor 4:2). Inverted CHAR-4 (VCG-03) produces moral deepening of the inversion: "their end is destruction" (Phili 3:19). Rev 16:15's call to vigilance frames CHAR-4's proper functioning as a sustained transformation project oriented toward Christ's coming. Reversibility: the functioning conscience can be restored; the inverted conscience's trajectory ("their end is destruction") is presented as non-reversible in its current direction.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — CHAR-5 produces transformation in two directions. (1) Destructive: sustained contempt deposits shame-identity (Bartimaeus's beggar-identity, Mar 10:50). (2) Redemptive: Jesus's reversal of contempt-verdicts (Act 4:11; 1Cor 1:28) transforms the despised into the chosen, overturning the contempt-system's accumulated verdict. The transformation is reversible in both directions: shame-identity can be abandoned (Mar 10:50 — throwing off the cloak); divine reversal can re-assign worth permanently.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — CHAR-6 produces the transformation of relational access: from the barrier of guilt-shame to the openness of approach to God. The person with clean hands and a blameless heart (Gen 20:5; Psa 26:6) moves toward God without the inner collapse that guilt-shame would produce. Conversely, the loss of innocence-capacity (Hos 8:5) produces the inverse transformation: from potential access to blocked access. Reversibility: maintained innocence (VCG-01) can be sustained through ongoing moral choices; lost innocence-capacity (Hos 8:5) requires divine intervention for restoration — it is not self-reversible once the capacity has been so deeply damaged.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster's transformative patterns fall into four trajectories. (1) Corrective transformation — shame and shamefulness identified as corrective signals that, when received, produce moral reorientation (Chars 1 M07-C, Char 4). Paradigm: 2Ch 30:15 — shame activating priestly consecration; Eze 43:10-11 — Israel's being-ashamed as the precondition for receiving the temple's full design. (2) Eschatological transformation — shame permanently removed and replaced by honour (Char 1's VCG-04 promises); mortal dishonour replaced by resurrection glory (Char 2 — 1Cor 15:43); contempt-verdict overturned by divine vindicating reversal (Char 5 — Act 4:11). (3) Identity transformation — the shame-identity abandoned in response to a higher worth-assignment (Char 5 — Bartimaeus throwing off the cloak; Act 4:11 — the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone). (4) Destructive transformation — the seared conscience, inverted conscience, and loss of innocence-capacity (Chars 1, 4, 6) as transformations in the destructive direction. The cluster's transformative range spans from the most redemptive (eschatological shame-removal) to the most catastrophic (the loss of the conscience's capacity to register moral reality).

**The primary forgiveness sequence (divine forgiveness received):**
- **Before:** Sin committed → guilt accumulated (the debt-state registered by conscience, confirmed by 54 shared verses with R073). The person is in the guilt-state — the legitimate claim stands against them.
- **Access-moment:** Repentance, faith, confession, intercession — the inner orientations through which the person moves toward reception.
- **During:** The divine act of releasing — "your sins are forgiven" (Luk 7:47-48). The moment of pronouncement/act.

- **After (sustained):** Hope (Psa 130:5-7); sustained love-orientation as relational disposition; capacity for horizontal forgiveness (F-003).

**The horizontal forgiveness sequence (human giving):**
- **Before:** Offence received → claim registered (moral awareness of legitimate grievance) → the inner state of withheld grievance (OBS-064-001 — "poisoning of the inner life").
- **Enabling moment:** Compassion (splagchnizomai, Mat 18:27); the heart-level decision to release.
- **During:** The act of forgiving — verbal declaration and/or inner release.
- **After:** Inner freedom from the retained grievance; the relational field reopened (F-008).

findings.session_b_note:
Yes — the data supports a reconstruction of the sequence, though it must be assembled from multiple passages rather than being stated in a single verse.

**In the giver:**

*Before:* The perceptive openness that allows seeing (T3.1). The eusplanchnos (tender heart) pre-condition (1 Pet 3:8, T2.5). A soul-level character disposition (chesed, ra.chum) that predisposes the person to be moved.

*During:* The gut-stirring of splanchnizō — the involuntary somatic event at the moment of perceiving need. The heart recoiling (Hos 11:8). The ni.chum warmth kindling. The volitional engagement that follows — the choice to act on or suppress the movement.

*After:* Outward action (healing, feeding, giving, touching). The eleēmosunē as the social form that sustains compassion-giving beyond the moment. For the character being formed: deepened eusplanchnos — the cycle of compassion-experience reinforcing the tenderness that enables future compassion.

**In the recipient (partial):**

*Before:* The pitiable condition (eleeinos) — need that has not yet been met.

*During:* The compassion-act reaching the person — bodily (Mark 1:41 — touch; Luke 7:14 — touch; Gen 19:16 — taken by the hand).

*After:* Changed condition (healed, fed, raised, rescued) and/or restored orientation (returned, comforted — Isa 57:18). The inner-being state following reception is largely silent, as established at T4.4.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-067-005: T5 as a whole reveals that goodness is one of the most developmentally rich characteristics in the programme. Three transformation types (condition change, orientation change, character transformation…
findings.finding_value: T5 as a whole reveals that goodness is one of the most developmentally rich characteristics in the programme. Three transformation types (condition change, orientation change, character transformation — Q&A-123), two distinct transformation sequences (positive encounter arc and moral awareness arc — Q&A-126), and three context-differentiated transformation mechanisms (encounter, Spirit-infusion, recognition-confrontation — Q&A-129) together produce a portrait of a characteristic that reaches the person through multiple developmental pathways depending on their condition and context. The formation/sanctification section confirms that goodness plays a dual developmental role: it is a product of formation (Spirit-formed character) and an agent of formation (the good person enables the formation of others — Q&A-136). The relationship to suffering deepens this: suffering is not incidental but a context in which goodness is deepened, revealed, tested, and even produced through confrontation with its absence (Q&A-133). T5.7 closes formally — no somatic deposit evidenced. The eschatological trajectory is present but underdeveloped in the data (Q&A-138-139).

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-011: T1's distinction between immediate response and sustained effect (Q&A-030) maps precisely onto T5's two transformation sequences (Q&A-126). The immediate response pattern (trust, praise, receptive des…
findings.finding_value: T1's distinction between immediate response and sustained effect (Q&A-030) maps precisely onto T5's two transformation sequences (Q&A-126). The immediate response pattern (trust, praise, receptive desire) corresponds to the initial stages of T5's positive arc (encounter → trust → refuge). The sustained effect (stable orientation, community capacity, settled disposition) corresponds to T5's later stages (reorientation → overflow → formation-agent capacity). Furthermore, T1's "sustained effect" (Q&A-028) identified stable inner orientation as the primary sustained product — T5 confirms this through the transformation to orientation change (Q&A-123) and the formation-agent role (Q&A-136). The two tiers read together reveal a temporal architecture for goodness: immediate contact produces first responses; sustained formation produces constitutive character; and the character-formed person becomes a formative resource for others.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-016: T2's constitutional movement (six-step sequence) and T5's transformation sequences (positive arc and moral awareness arc) describe the same developmental reality from two analytical perspectives. T2 d…
findings.finding_value: T2's constitutional movement (six-step sequence) and T5's transformation sequences (positive arc and moral awareness arc) describe the same developmental reality from two analytical perspectives. T2 describes where goodness moves in the person (constitutional levels); T5 describes how goodness moves the person (mechanisms and sequences). The six-step T2 sequence (Spirit → soul → heart → volition → agency → expression) is the constitutional substrate through which T5's transformation arcs operate. T5's three mechanisms (encounter, Spirit-infusion, recognition-confrontation) are the relational/contextual triggers that activate the T2 constitutional movement. Together: the T2 constitutional architecture provides the vertical structure through which T5's developmental arcs run. Formation is not a disembodied process — it is the progressive deepening of goodness through the constitutional levels identified in T2.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-023: T4 identified that God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional while the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional (Q&A-100). T5 named the transformation arcs t…
findings.finding_value: T4 identified that God's goodness as a character attribute is unconditional while the human's ongoing experience of its relational benefits is conditional (Q&A-100). T5 named the transformation arcs through which the conditional dimension operates: the positive transformation arc (encounter → trust → reorientation → overflow) is the arc in which the conditional relational experience is deepened; the moral awareness arc (recognition → loathing → repentance) is the arc that recovers the relational experience when it has been lost through departure. T4's human-to-God enabling inner postures (waiting, seeking, trust — Q&A-104) correspond to T5's formation mechanisms: the posture of waiting corresponds to the encounter mechanism (sustained receptive openness); the moral awareness arc is the recovery mechanism for the person who has departed from the relational posture. Together: T5's formative processes are the mechanisms through which T4's relational conditions are entered, sustained, and restored. Transformation and relationship are inseparable in goodness.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-067-026: T5 confirmed that goodness plays a dual developmental role — formation product and formation agent (Q&A-136). T6 confirmed that the characteristics most closely connected to goodness in co-occurrence …
findings.finding_value: T5 confirmed that goodness plays a dual developmental role — formation product and formation agent (Q&A-136). T6 confirmed that the characteristics most closely connected to goodness in co-occurrence and shared anchors are the same characteristics named in the transformation arcs. The Gal 5:22 shared anchors (love, joy, patience, peace, faith) are the characteristics that co-occur in the context of Spirit-produced formation (the fruit list). The Mic 6:8 shared anchors (justice, kindness, love, humility) are the characteristics that are co-constituted with goodness in the definition of the formed human moral life. The cross-registry connections (T6) are the structural record of what characteristics goodness produces in others when it acts as a formation agent (T5). R103 (love) as the highest co-occurrence connection (T6.1 — 28 shared verses) is also the characteristic most naturally produced by encounter with goodness in the positive transformation arc — goodness → trust and love as natural co-products. T5's formation-agent role has T6's cross-registry connections as its structural trace in the programme.

findings.finding_value: Love's formation operates through a multi-layered process in the data. The primary pathway is receptive: divine love received (1Jo 4:19) → Spirit infusion (Rom 5:5, Gal 5:22) → heart-reception → soul-response → community expression. Secondary pathways: obedience → soul purification → sincere love (1Pe 1:22); forgiveness received → love generated (Luk 7:47 — via SD-020); training within community (Tit 2:4). Love can grow (1Th 3:12) and increase through the Lord's action. Its reversibility is asymmetric: divine love is irreversible by nature (Jer 31:3 — everlasting; Lam 3:22 — never ceasing); human love is subject to redirection through competing love-allegiances (2Ti 4:10 — Demas). The eschatological trajectory is toward perfection and direct knowledge: partial now (mediated by community, neighbour-teaching), moving toward fullness (perfect love casting out fear — 1Jo 4:18; direct divine knowledge — Jer 31:34; pleasures forevermore — Psa 16:11). Formation requires community — love cannot be formed in isolation; it requires both the divine giver and the human community as the formation context.
