findings.finding_value: M01-A is the most eschatologically oriented sub-group. Rev 11:18 (fearing God's name as the defining characteristic of those who receive reward at the final judgment); Rev 14:7 (fearing God commanded in view of "the hour of his judgment" — an eschatological framing); Rev 15:4 (fearing the Lord portrayed as "the universal, inevitable response to his holiness and revealed righteous acts" — eschatological universalisation of reverential fear); Rev 19:5 (fearing God as the defining characteristic of his servants called to praise him at the consummation). The fullness of M01-A is the eschatological state in which all creation — redeemed humanity, living creatures, the nations — fears God in unified reverential worship.

M01-B's eschatological orientation is the freedom from all disordering fear: Rev 2:10 (M01-B-VCG-06/F-VCG-05: commanded not to fear the coming suffering — the faithful endurance through eschatological trial); Luk 21:26 (M01-B-VCG-03: cosmic signs producing fainting from fear — eschatological fear as the context for the "do not be frightened" commands of Luk 21:9 anchor).

M01-D's eschatological direction is the promise of no-more-dismay: Jer 30:10 (anchor D-VCG-04: "dismay is the inner collapse God forbids Israel to experience — the assurance of salvation and quiet rest is set as the direct antidote"); eschatological fullness as the state of undismayed composure grounded in God's salvation.

M01-E-VCG-03/04 show eschatological promise through the restoration corpus: Eze 34:28 (M01-E-VCG-03: "none shall make them afraid" — the restored flock free from fear-trembling); Mic 4:4 (anchor E-VCG-04: "no one will make anyone afraid — the ideal future is one where the inner person is wholly free from the threat-driven dread that now afflicts them").

M01-F's eschatological direction: Heb 2:15 (Christ's deliverance from lifelong fear-of-death slavery — an eschatological liberation from the most pervasive form of chronic dread); 1Jo 4:18 (perfect love casting out fear — the fullness of M01-F's resolution is the love-perfected state in which no punishment-anticipatory fear remains).

M01-G's eschatological direction: Rev 21:8 (cowardice leading to the lake of fire — the negative eschatological terminus of sustained timidity); by contrast, the positive is the faithfulness that characterises the redeemed (Rev 11:18; 19:5 — the God-fearers, not the cowards, receive the eschatological reward).

The cluster's eschatological fullness is a state in which: reverential fear of God is universal, perfected, and permanent (M01-A, Rev corpus); all disordering fears (threat, death, punishment-anticipation) are removed (M01-B, F, G); and the freedom from fear-of-harm is the mark of the redeemed condition (M01-D, E restoration corpus). The cluster points consistently toward an eschatological state of purified, universal, undistorted fear of God — and freedom from every other fear.

Yes. The eschatological-wrath corpus (M02-A-VCG-02) is definitionally eschatological: Rev 19:15 (the wrath behind the winepress of final judgment) is the fullness toward which all historical expressions of wrath point. 1Th 5:9 (M02-A-VCG-02): "God's purpose for believers is not wrath but salvation" — the eschatological destiny of the redeemed is specifically the negation of wrath, toward which the present deliverance from wrath points.

Yes. The eschatological-wrath corpus (M02-A-VCG-02) is definitionally eschatological: Rev 19:15 (the wrath behind the winepress of final judgment) is the fullness toward which all historical expressions of wrath point. 1Th 5:9 (M02-A-VCG-02): "God's purpose for believers is not wrath but salvation" — the eschatological destiny of the redeemed is specifically the negation of wrath, toward which the present deliverance from wrath points.

Divine jealousy's eschatological trajectory is restorative: Joe 2:18 (M02-E-VCG-02) shows God's jealousy turning from judgment to restorative action; Isa 9:7 (M02-E-VCG-02) shows zeal as the inner driving force behind the establishing of the promised kingdom — the fullness toward which divine jealousy moves is the permanent, unrivalled reign of righteousness.
Isa 11:13 (M02-E-VCG-04): inter-tribal jealousy abolished in the messianic age — destructive competitive jealousy is eschatologically eliminated. The fullness is a community without covetous envy.

Yes, and this is one of M03's most pervasive and structurally significant patterns. The eschatological trajectory of grief is present across all sub-groups. Sighing and sorrow flee when everlasting joy arrives (Isa 35:10, 51:11 — M03-E-VCG-03; M03-C-VCG-01). God wipes every tear from every face (Isa 25:8 — M03-A-VCG-02). Weeping ceases in restored Jerusalem (Isa 65:19 — M03-A-VCG-05). Mourning shall be no more (Rev 21:4 — M03-B-VCG-04). Pain shall be no more (Rev 21:4 — BOUNDARY). Creation's groan is oriented toward future redemption (Rom 8:22 — M03-E-VCG-02). The eschatological trajectory of M03 is not that grief simply ends but that its ending is the measure of the fullness of restoration — what grief describes is the absence of what the fullness will supply.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, strongly. The eschatological concentration of exultation passages is one of the most notable features of the corpus: Isa 65:18 (forever exultation in God's new creation); Isa 65:19 (God's own exultation in the new Jerusalem); Isa 66:10 (all who love Jerusalem exulting in her restoration); Jer 32:41 (God's new-covenant exultation over Israel); Zep 3:17 (God exulting with loud singing over his people in the final restoration); Zec 9:9 (Zion exulting at her king's coming). The eschatological fullness of exultation is both the human exultation at God's final acts and God's own exultation over his fully restored people.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, this is one of the most prominent features of Characteristic 2. (1) **Fullness of Joy as eschatological goal** — Joh 15:11 ("your joy may be full"); Joh 16:24 ("that your joy may be full" through asking in Jesus' name); 1Jo 1:4; 2Jo 12 (joy made complete through communion); (2) **Everlasting Joy** — Isa 35:10; 51:11 ("everlasting joy shall be upon their heads"); Isa 61:7 ("everlasting joy"); (3) **Irremovable Joy** — Joh 16:22 ("no one will take your joy from you"); (4) **Eschatological event Joy** — Rev 19:7 (commanded corporate Joy at the Lamb's marriage); Mat 25:21, 23 (entering the master's Joy as final reward); Jude 24 (presented before God's glory "with great joy"); (5) **OT restoration Joy** — M04-E-VCG-01 throughout — the entire sa.s.von corpus is eschatologically oriented.

**[CHAR-7]** E — Yes, this is constitutive of the characteristic's structure: (1) **Reward in heaven** — Mat 5:12 ("your reward is great in heaven"); (2) **Glory at revelation** — 1Pe 4:13 ("that you may also rejoice and be glad when his glory is revealed"); (3) **Inexpressible and glorious** — 1Pe 1:8 ("joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory") — the present joy already participates in the eschatological quality of glory; (4) **Christ's joy fully realised** — Heb 12:2 (the joy set before Christ → now seated at the right hand) — the eschatological resolution of his suffering-joy is the pattern and promise for the believer's; (5) **Lamb's marriage** — Rev 19:7 (agalliao in the eschatological wedding celebration — the final and unqualified form of the joy that present Suffering-Joy anticipates).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Partially — less strongly than Joy (Characteristic 2). The covenantal-promise register (M04-O-VCG-04: Jer 29:10; 33:14; Jos 21:45) shows Gladness anchored in promise-fulfilment, which has an eschatological dimension. The ki-tov declarations ("for his steadfast love endures forever") orient Gladness toward the eternal character of God's goodness. Lam 3:25–26 (waiting for the salvation of the Lord) has an eschatological orientation. The makarismos passages (Rom 4:6, 9; Gal 4:15) point to the blessedness declared in Christ as an eschatological state already received. However, compared to Joy's extensive "everlasting joy" and "fullness of joy" vocabulary, Gladness's eschatological orientation is present but less concentrated.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes, significantly: (1) **Isa 62:4** — "you shall be called My Delight Is in Her" — God's Delight in Zion as eschatological name and identity; (2) **Mal 3:12** — "you will be a land of delight" — the restored community as a delight-characterized eschatological state; (3) **Isa 58:14** — "then you shall take delight in the Lord, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth" — Sabbath faithfulness leading to eschatological Delight-in-God and divine exaltation; (4) **Job 22:26** — "then you will delight yourself in the Almighty" — the restored person's future Delight in the Almighty; (5) **Isa 11:8** — sha.a in the messianic age (nursing child playing over cobra's hole) — the carefree Delight of the eschatological peace when fear is removed; (6) **Luk 12:32** — "it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom" — the eschatological gift driven by divine eudokeo.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes: (1) **Psa 16:11** — "at your right hand are pleasures forevermore" — the most explicit eschatological Pleasure statement in the corpus: pleasures in God's permanent presence; (2) **Eze 20:41** — future divine acceptance as pleasing aroma — eschatological restoration of the worship-Pleasure relationship; (3) **Psa 36:8** — "river of your delights" as the eschatological supply in God's house (anticipating the river of life — Rev 22:1); (4) **Zec 8:19** — former fasts becoming cheerful feasts — the eschatological transformation of communal mourning into Pleasure; (5) **Job 36:11** — years of pleasantness as the outcome of faithful service — anticipating the fullness of pleasantness in the age of complete justice.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes: (1) **Isa 29:14** ("I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder") — the escalating wonder of God's future acts as an eschatological promise; (2) **Mic 7:15** ("as in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show them marvellous things") — new-Exodus wonders as eschatological fullness; (3) **Isa 9:6** ("his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor") — the coming child's wonder-name as the eschatological fullness of all divine wonder-acts; (4) **Dan 12:6** ("how long till the end of these wonders?") — apocalyptic wonders as transitional to the final age; (5) **Isa 25:1** ("wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure") — God's ancient purposes being revealed in wonder as the eschatological disclosure.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All seven have eschatological trajectories, but with markedly different eschatological intensity: (1) **Most constitutively eschatological**: Suffering-Joy (Char 7) — eschatological grounding is definitional; the present form is inherently transitional (toward the glory-joy of 1Pe 4:13); Joy (Char 2) — "everlasting joy" (Isa 35:10; 51:11), "no one will take your joy from you" (Joh 16:22), the fullness-of-Joy Johannine vocabulary; (2) **Strongly eschatological**: Exultation (Char 1) — the Isaianic new-creation exultation passages (Isa 65:18–19; 66:10; Zep 3:17 in the final-restoration context); Delight (Char 4) — the renamed Zion "My Delight Is in Her" (Isa 62:4); the "land of delight" (Mal 3:12); Wonder (Char 6) — "wonder upon wonder" (Isa 29:14); the Wonderful Counselor's eschatological fullness; (3) **Present-weighted with eschatological horizon**: Gladness (Char 3) — less concentrated eschatological vocabulary than Joy; more characteristically present-responsive but with covenantal-promise grounding; Pleasure (Char 5) — "pleasures forevermore" (Psa 16:11); river of delights anticipating the river of life. The cluster as a whole is eschatologically oriented: all seven point toward a future fullness that surpasses their present forms. The cluster cannot be fully understood without its eschatological dimension.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, strongly. The M07-A-VCG-04 material is the primary evidence: Isa 54:4 — "you will not be ashamed... you will forget the shame of your youth... the reproach of your widowhood you will remember no more"; Isa 61:7 — "instead of your shame there shall be a double portion... they shall have everlasting joy"; Joe 2:26 — "my people shall never again be put to shame"; Zep 3:19 — "I will change their shame into praise and renown in all the earth." The M07-C-VCG-04 material extends this eschatologically: Isa 45:17 — "never be put to shame or confounded to all eternity"; Joe 2:27 — "my people shall never again be put to shame." Rev 3:18 (vc=34975) — the naked shame covered by Christ's garments — frames the present shame-condition within eschatological transformation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, strongly. (1) The Day-of-the-Lord material (Isa 2:9-17; 13:11) points toward eschatological completion. (2) 1Cor 15:43 — body sown in dishonor, raised in glory — is the eschatological resolution of CHAR-2 at the individual level. (3) Hab 2:16 — "utter shame will come upon your glory" — is directed eschatologically: God's cup of judgment will finally execute the complete reversal of all proud human standing.

---

**[CHAR-3]** E — The structural-dishonour mode (VCG-02) points toward its own eschatological resolution: 2Ti 2:20's vessel for dishonorable use is implicitly oriented toward the possibility of cleansing (2:21 context). Rom 9:21's potter-and-clay raises the deepest eschatological question: sovereign assignment of dishonour-standings as a condition of creaturely existence, and whether eschatological transformation re-assigns those standings.

---

**[CHAR-4]** E — Rev 16:15 frames CHAR-4's proper functioning as oriented toward the moment of Christ's coming: the one who "stays awake, keeping his garments on" avoids the shame of exposure at that moment. The eschatological fullness is the state in which moral vigilance has been sustained and the shameful has been renounced throughout — so that at Christ's coming no exposure occurs. CHAR-4's eschatological trajectory is toward the full activation and correct calibration of the moral-evaluative conscience.

---

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. Act 4:11 (the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone) is the paradigmatic eschatological statement of CHAR-5's reversal. 1Cor 1:28 (God choosing the despised to nullify things that are) is the eschatological programme: the world's contempt-verdicts are being overturned, and this overturning will be completed in the eschaton. The present experience of CHAR-5 anticipates its final reversal — shame from contempt is a temporary condition oriented toward the vindicating re-worth-assignment of God.

---

**[CHAR-6]** E — Psa 73:13's lament — maintained innocence apparently futile — is resolved in its wider context by the sanctuary encounter and the eschatological vindication of the righteous. The present experience of CHAR-6 (maintained innocence under suffering) anticipates its eschatological vindication: the person who maintains moral integrity will find it vindicated when "their end" is seen clearly (Psa 73:17). The eschatological fullness is the state in which innocence's protective function is fully confirmed and the wicked's apparently successful rejection of it is finally judged.

---

**[CLUSTER]** E — At the cluster level, M07's eschatological trajectory is toward the permanent resolution of all shame-producing conditions and the full restoration of inner standing, worth, and innocence that shame has violated. The most explicit statements: Char 1 (Isa 54:4; 61:7; Joe 2:26-27 — shame removed, replaced by double portion and everlasting joy; Isa 45:17 — never put to shame to all eternity), Char 2 (1Cor 15:43 — dishonored body raised in glory), Chars 3 and 5 (God's final correct worth-assignment overturning all contempt-verdicts), Char 4 (Rev 16:15 — the vigilant maintaining of conscience toward Christ's coming), Char 6 (Psa 73's lament resolved in the sanctuary pointing toward final vindication). Cluster-level picture of the eschatological fullness: no unjust shame remains; no proud humiliation is needed because pride has been finally corrected; all worth is correctly assigned; all conscience is fully calibrated to God's standard; all contempt-verdicts are overturned; all moral integrity is vindicated. M07's eschatological orientation is the most comprehensive in the programme for the promise-density directed at a single inner-being domain.

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes — but toward eschatological reversal, not fullness. The day-of-the-Lord material in M08-A3-VCG-04 constitutes the primary eschatological evidence: Isa 2:12 (vc=33957, vc=65778, M08-A3-VCG-04) — "the Lord of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up — and it shall be brought low" — CHAR-1 as the comprehensive target of the eschatological day. Isa 2:11 (vc=34089, vc=34601): "the haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted in that day" — CHAR-1's universal humbling as the eschatological event. Eze 31:14 (vc=54400, M08-A3-VCG-04): "God's judgment is designed to prevent any future tree from aspiring to such elevation, ending the cycle of proud growth" — the eschatological terminus of CHAR-1 is not fullness but permanent closure of the cycle. Pro 16:18 (vc=34073, M08-A1-VCG-03): "pride goes before destruction" — the structural eschatological trajectory of CHAR-1 is toward destruction, not toward fullness.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Toward eschatological destruction, not fullness. Mal 4:1 (vc=34107, M08-B-VCG-02): "the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble; the day that is coming shall set them ablaze... it will leave them neither root nor branch" — total eschatological destruction as CHAR-2's terminus. Jer 50:31–32 (vc=34116/34117, M08-B-VCG-02): Babylon ("the most proud one," "arrogance") — "the proud one stumbles and falls, and none will raise him up" — the irreversible fall at the national scale anticipating the eschatological.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes — uniquely among M08 characteristics, CHAR-3's VCG-03 form has a positive eschatological orientation. 1Th 2:19 (vc=33913, M08-C-VCG-03): "what is our hope or joy or crown of boasting before our Lord Jesus at his coming? Is it not you?" — the community-boasting is explicitly eschatological, oriented toward Christ's parousia. Phili 2:16 (vc=33910, M08-C-VCG-03): "my pride on the day of Christ" — the examined boasting is oriented toward the eschatological day. 2Cor 1:14 (vc=33907, M08-C-VCG-03): mutual boasting "on the day of our Lord Jesus."

**[CHAR-4]** E — Toward eschatological judgment, not fullness. 2Ti 3:4 (vc=33926, M08-D-VCG-02): tufoō (being swollen with conceit) in the end-times vice character list — CHAR-4 as a characteristic of the eschatological final days' moral collapse. 1Ti 3:6 (vc=33924, M08-D-VCG-02): "the condemnation of the devil" as the judicial trajectory — the eschatological endpoint is condemnation, not fullness.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Toward eschatological desolation and shame, not fullness. Eze 33:28 (vc=33999, M08-E-VCG-01): "proud might shall come to an end" as the eschatological trajectory of all national power-pride. Jer 51:53 (vc=65670, M08-E-VCG-02): even the highest fortification Babylon could build cannot prevent divine judgment. Hab 2:9 (vc=34169, M08-E-VCG-02): "shame on him who builds his house by unjust gain" — shame, not security, is the eschatological end. Lev 26:19 (vc=33982, M08-E-VCG-01): God will "break the pride of your power" — eschatological breaking.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The eschatological trajectories across the five reveal M08's predominantly negative eschatological orientation. CHAR-1: day-of-the-Lord judgment and universal humbling (Isa 2:12, M08-A3-VCG-04). CHAR-2: eschatological fire consuming the arrogant (Mal 4:1, M08-B-VCG-02). CHAR-3 VCG-01: elimination — "no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1Cor 1:29, M08-C-VCG-01); VCG-02/03: positive eschatological boasting before Christ (1Th 2:19, M08-C-VCG-03; Phili 2:16, M08-C-VCG-03). CHAR-4: judicial condemnation (1Ti 3:6, M08-D-VCG-02) and end-times vice catalogue (2Ti 3:4, M08-D-VCG-02). CHAR-5: desolation and shame (Eze 33:28, M08-E-VCG-01; Hab 2:9, M08-E-VCG-02). The cluster-synthesis: M08's eschatological horizon is predominantly negative — four of five characteristics (and CHAR-3's VCG-01 form) move toward judgment, reversal, and destruction. Only CHAR-3's examined/God-directed registers have a positive eschatological orientation.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, explicitly. Gen49:10 — "to him shall be the obedience of the peoples" — an eschatological gathering of all nations in submission to the coming ruler. Rom16:26 — "the obedience of faith" as the telos of gospel disclosure to all nations — the eschatological goal of the entire apostolic mission. Heb5:9 — Christ "became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him" — the eschatological salvation is mediated through and to the obedient. 2Th1:8 — those who do not obey the gospel face eschatological judgment — the obedience characteristic is the criterion at the eschatological divide. The characteristic has a fully articulated eschatological trajectory: toward the universal submission of all peoples to Christ's authority, and as the inner condition for receiving eschatological salvation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Isa57:15 carries eschatological resonance in the Isaianic context — the high-and-holy God who inhabits eternity names his dwelling with the contrite as a consistent feature of his character and action. In the broader Isaianic context, this points toward the eschatological reality of God's dwelling with his people in renewed intimacy. The reviving of spirit and heart (Isa57:15) anticipates the eschatological resurrection-life in which broken humanity is fully revived. However, within the two-verse corpus alone, the eschatological dimension is present in resonance rather than explicit statement.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Heb5:2's typological dimension (T0.4.1) — the Aaronic high priest as type pointing toward Christ as superior high priest — carries an implicit eschatological trajectory: the present form of priestly metriopatheō anticipates its eschatological fullness in Christ's perfect compassionate mediation. The Hebrews context (Heb4:15 — outside corpus — "we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses") points toward the eschatological fulfillment of the high priestly metriopatheō in Christ's perfect priestly empathy. Within §3.C alone, this is present as implicit typological trajectory rather than explicit statement.

**[CHAR-5]** S — The three-verse corpus does not directly evidence an eschatological trajectory for semnotēs. The characteristic is addressed in present-community contexts without explicit eschatological framing.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The tabernacle-offering contexts (Exo35:5/22) carry typological-eschatological resonance (T0.4.1): the free-will offering for God's dwelling place points toward the eschatological fullness of willing-hearted devotion in the renewed creation. Psa51:12's prayer for a willing spirit — seeking what has been lost — anticipates the eschatological fullness in which the willing spirit is permanent rather than fragile and recoverable. In NT terms (outside corpus but as typological trajectory), the Spirit-given willing orientation of the new covenant community anticipates an eschatological fullness of joyful freely-given devotion.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, in multiple registers. *The exaltation-at-the-proper-time promise:* 1Pe5:6 — "humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you" — the eschatological exaltation is the promised fullness toward which present humbling is oriented. Mat23:12 — "whoever humbles himself will be exalted" — the exaltation is the telos of the present posture. *The bodily transformation:* Phili3:21 — "who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body" — the present creaturely lowliness (M09-B condition) is explicitly oriented toward a future transformation into conformity with Christ's glorified state. The characteristic has a present form (voluntary self-lowering and experienced lowliness) and a future fullness (divine exaltation and bodily transformation), with the present pointing toward the future.

**[CLUSTER]** E — The cluster has a graduated eschatological profile: two characteristics with strong explicit eschatological orientation, one with implicit typological trajectory, two with resonance only, one with silence. *Explicit*: CHAR-2 Submission is the cluster's most eschatologically saturated characteristic — Gen49:10, Rom16:26, 2Th1:8, and the universal-submission telos make it the cluster's primary eschatological carrier. CHAR-1 Humility: the exaltation-of-the-humble pattern and Phili3:21 (bodily transformation) provide explicit eschatological orientation. *Implicit typological*: CHAR-4 Meekness — through the Aaronic-to-Christological priestly sequence (Heb5:2 → Heb4:15). *Resonance*: CHAR-3 Contrition (Isa57:15's reviving anticipating fullness) and CHAR-6 Willing-heartedness (tabernacle-type pointing toward permanent willing spirit). *Silent*: CHAR-5 Dignity — no eschatological trajectory in its three-verse corpus. Cluster-level: M09's eschatological vision is anchored in CHAR-2 — the universal submission of all peoples to Christ is the cluster's ultimate horizon. CHAR-1's exaltation-pattern is the individual's eschatological orientation; CHAR-2's universal submission is the cosmic eschatological orientation. Together they describe M09's eschatological scope: from individual reversal (CHAR-1) to universal gathering (CHAR-2).

---

**[CHAR-1]** E — Limited eschatological evidence is present. Joh 5:14 ("sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you") implies that there is a final reckoning toward which sinning trajectories move — "nothing worse" opens an eschatological dimension of consequence. 2Pe 2:4 ("committed to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment") shows that the angels who sinned are being held for a final judgment — the eschatological reckoning is the horizon toward which sinning accountability moves. Eze 18:4/20 ("the soul who sins shall die") has an eschatological dimension in its ultimacy — the mortal consequence is final.

**[CHAR-10]** E — Yes — toward eschatological judgment for enticement. 2Pe 2:14 — "Accursed children!" — the eschatological trajectory for the enticers is divine curse-judgment. The broader 2Pe 2 context (not all in the 5-verse corpus) makes explicit that the false teachers face divine judgment as their eschatological end. For apostasy: Act 21:21's covenantal framework is itself oriented toward the new-covenant fulfillment in Christ — the broader Acts narrative situates the apostasy-accusation within the eschatological-theological movement from the Mosaic covenant to the new covenant.

**[CHAR-11]** E — Yes — toward two opposed eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment for those remaining in the condition*: Joh 8:21/24 — "you will die in your sin... you will die in your sins" — the eschatological consequence of remaining in the condition is death-in-the-condition (permanent separation from where Jesus goes); Mal 4:1 — "all evildoers will be stubble. The day that is coming shall set them ablaze" — the condition's wickedness-register (VCG-01) faces the Day of the Lord's consuming fire. 1Th 2:16 — "wrath has come upon them at last" — accumulated sin reaches its full measure and triggers final judgment. (2) *Eternal life for those freed from the condition*: Rom 6:22 — "the fruit you get leads to sanctification and its end, eternal life" — liberation from the condition is oriented toward eternal life as the eschatological fullness of the positive direction.

**[CHAR-12]** E — Yes — two opposed eschatological endpoints. (1) *Negative — sin unto death*: 1Jo 5:16 — "there is sin that leads to death" — the enslaving power in its most entrenched form has an eschatological terminus of death; prayer cannot reach this endpoint. (2) *Positive — destruction of the devil's works*: 1Jo 3:8 — "the reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil" — the enslaving power's grounding in the devil's works is eschatologically oriented toward the Son of God's destruction of those works; the enslaving power is not permanent but is being actively destroyed. (3) *Positive — the evil one does not touch*: 1Jo 5:18 — the born-of-God state of non-enslavement is the eschatological trajectory of the liberated person; the evil one's inability to touch names the positive fullness toward which the liberation moves.

**[CHAR-13]** E — Yes — two opposed eschatological endpoints. (1) *The new-covenant erasure*: Jer 31:34 — "I will remember their sin no more" — the eschatological fullness of the new covenant is the permanent divine non-remembrance of the sin-record; Dan 9:24 — "seventy weeks are decreed... to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness" — the record's complete termination and the installation of everlasting righteousness; (2) *Eschatological visitation*: Exo 32:34 — "in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them"; Hos 13:12 — "his sin is kept in store" — the sealed record awaits its appointed day of reckoning; Jer 14:10 — "he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins" — the deferred record has a final judgment appointment.

**[CHAR-14]** E — Yes — the OT provisional system explicitly points toward the eschatological fullness. (1) *The annual cycle's forward orientation*: Exo 30:10 — "once in the year throughout your generations" — the generational repetition implies an endpoint where the annual repetition will no longer be necessary; the cycle points toward its own completion; (2) *The new-covenant blood*: Mat 26:28 — "this is my blood of the covenant... for the forgiveness of sins" — the new covenant's blood-forgiveness is the eschatological fulfillment that the annual kip.pu.rim cycle anticipated; (3) *Dan 9:24 (CHAR-13 corpus)*: "to put an end to sin, and to atone for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness" — the eschatological atonement is the final fullness toward which all provisional atonement pointed.

**[CHAR-15]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Positive — divine cleansing and covenant restoration*: Eze 37:23 — "I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — the eschatological fullness is the complete cleansing of the accumulated generational backsliding and the restored covenant-people identity; (2) *Negative — eschatological curse*: Isa 65:20 — "the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed" — within the new-creation context of Isa 65, the sinner who persists in the sinning-pattern (even across a hundred years) faces the eschatological verdict of curse rather than blessing.

**[CHAR-16]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment and destruction*: Isa 13:9 — "to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it" — the sinner-identity's eschatological destination under divine wrath; Psa 104:35 — "let sinners be consumed from the earth"; Isa 1:28 — "rebels and sinners shall be broken together"; Jude 15 — "to execute judgment on all... ungodly sinners"; (2) *Repentance and cosmic joy*: Luk 15:7/10 — the sinner who repents generates heavenly joy; Psa 51:13 — "sinners will return to you" — eschatological return of sinners to God; Amo 9:8 — "except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob" — within the sinful kingdom's judgment, a remnant is preserved.

**[CHAR-17]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment enforcement of accumulated guilt*: Eze 21:25 — "the time of your final punishment" — the guilt-state has an appointed eschatological day of enforcement; Isa 24:6 — "inhabitants suffer for their guilt" in the earth's final desolation; (2) *Complete cleansing*: Jer 33:8 — "I will cleanse them from all the guilt of their sin against me, and I will forgive all the guilt" — the eschatological fullness is the total removal of all accumulated guilt; Hos 5:15 — God's return after guilt-acknowledgment anticipates the final restoration in which guilt's barrier between God and people is permanently removed.

**[CHAR-18]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment enforcement of accumulated iniquity*: Gen 15:16 — the Amorites' accumulation is moving toward its appointed threshold; Isa 13:11 — "I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity"; Isa 26:21 — the Lord coming to punish the earth's inhabitants for their iniquity; (2) *Total removal*: Jer 50:20 — "iniquity shall be sought in Israel, and there shall be none... for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant" — the eschatological fullness is the complete dissolution of the iniquity-record; Zec 3:9 — "I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day"; Jer 31:34 — "I will remember their sin no more" — God's memory of iniquity permanently cleared.

**[CHAR-19]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment and finish*: Dan 9:24 — "seventy weeks are decreed... to finish the transgression, to put an end to sin" — transgression has a divinely decreed completion-point; Dan 8:23 — "when the transgressors have reached their limit, a king of bold face shall arise" — the eschatological crisis follows transgression reaching its maximum; Isa 66:24 — "their worm shall not die, their fire shall not be quenched" — the persistent rebels' eschatological state; (2) *Complete removal*: Isa 43:25 — "I will not remember your sins"; Psa 103:12 — as far as east from west; Eze 18:22 — "none of the transgressions... shall be remembered against him" — forgiven transgressions have no eschatological standing.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The Ezekiel cultic-purification corpus (VCG-02: Eze 43:20/22; 45:18) is located within Ezekiel's eschatological temple vision — the restored sanctuary of the age to come. The annual sanctuary purification (Eze 45:18 — "in the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take a bull from the herd without blemish and purify the sanctuary") in an eschatological context suggests that a purification-from-sin mechanism remains in view in the restored order. Whether this represents the continuation of inadvertent-sinning dynamics in the eschaton or a symbolic-anticipatory language is not resolved within the 18-verse corpus. The eschatological orientation is present: the purification of the sacred space points toward a finally and comprehensively cleansed sanctuary.

**[CHAR-20]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment endpoint*: 1Ch 10:13 — "Saul died for his breach of faith" — death as faithlessness's personal eschatological verdict; Dan 9:7 — exile and open shame as the communal eschatological judgment; 2Ch 30:7 — "made them a desolation" — desolation as the nation's judgment; (2) *Restoration endpoint*: Eze 39:26 — "they shall forget their shame and all the treachery they have practiced against me, when they dwell securely in their land with none to make them afraid" — the eschatological fullness is secure dwelling in which the shame of treachery is forgotten; Lev 26:42 — "I will remember my covenant" — covenant-memory restoration as the eschatological goal.

**[CHAR-21]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment of the perverting agent*: Rev 19:2 — "he has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth" — the cosmic-scale corruption agent faces God's true and just judgment; 1Cor 3:17 — "God will destroy him" who destroys the temple; Pro 10:31 — "the perverse tongue will be cut off"; (2) *Liberation from corruption*: Rom 8:21 — "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption and obtain the freedom of the glory of the children of God" — the eschatological fullness for CHAR-21 is the cosmic liberation from corruption; 2Pe 1:4 — having escaped from the corruption into divine nature as the individual eschatological orientation.

**[CHAR-22]** E — Yes — two eschatological endpoints. (1) *Judgment of the unjust*: 2Pe 2:9 — "keep the unrighteous under punishment until the day of judgment" — current custody awaiting final judgment; Rev 18:5 — God remembers Babylon's accumulated iniquities awaiting judgment; 1Cor 6:9 — "the unrighteous will not inherit the kingdom of God" — the definitive eschatological exclusion; (2) *Total elimination of injustice in the remnant*: Zep 3:13 — "those who are left in Israel shall do no injustice and speak no lies" — the eschatological fullness is the community that no longer practices injustice; Mat 5:45 — "sends rain on the just and on the unjust" — even common grace extends to the unjust until the eschatological separation.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Limited but present eschatological evidence. Mic 7:9 — "I will bear the indignation of the Lord because I have sinned against him, *until* he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication" — confession is here positioned as a present posture ("I will bear") oriented toward a future vindication ("he will bring me out to the light"). The confession does not end the moral episode; it positions the confessor toward a future divine resolution. Eze 33:16 — "he shall surely live" — points toward a future of life beyond the sin that required confession. The eschatological frame is implicit: confession is the present-tense posture that positions the person toward God's future vindication and life.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes — toward *judgment* as its eschatological trajectory. Jer 2:35 — "Behold, I will bring you to judgment for saying, 'I have not sinned'" — the judgment announced is the eschatological direction of conscience suppression: the suppressed inner accountability before God will surface in external divine judgment. Tit 3:11 — "he is self-condemned" — the self-condemnation that the conscience-suppressed person does not consciously receive now anticipates an outer condemnation that will confirm the inner verdict. The eschatological trajectory of conscience suppression is toward a judgment that cannot itself be suppressed — the divine reckoning that the inner moral witness has already pronounced but the person has refused to hear.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes — toward judgment as its eschatological trajectory, in increasingly sharp terms. Eze 18:24 — "for them he shall die" — the death-consequence points toward a final divine verdict on the person who persistently sinned without turning back. Heb 10:26–27 (the broader context of 10:26's "no sacrifice remaining") — "a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries" — names the eschatological horizon of refusal to repent: the person who deliberately persists in sinning after knowing truth faces judgment as the final state. The eschatological fullness toward which refusal to repent points is the divine judgment that cannot itself be refused.

**[CHAR-6]** E — The corpus points habitual defection toward judgment and loss as its eschatological trajectory. Pro 11:31 — "how much more the wicked and the sinner!" — the sinner faces amplified eschatological recompense. Heb 3:17 — "whose bodies fell in the wilderness" — the wilderness generation's sustained habitual sinning culminated in physical death-in-the-desert; the eschatological frame of the Hebrews argument implies this as a type of the more severe judgment awaiting those who repeat the pattern. 1Sa 2:25 — "it was the will of the Lord to put them to death" — divine resolution to judge Eli's sons' habitual sinning points toward an irreversible eschatological verdict.

**[CHAR-7]** E — The corpus points contagious sin toward two eschatological trajectories. (1) *Judgment and abandonment*: 1Ki 14:16 — "he will give Israel up because of the sins of Jeroboam" — the ultimate consequence of sustained contagious sin transmission across generations is national abandonment by God; the exile of the Northern Kingdom is the eschatological endpoint of the Jeroboam transmission. (2) *Structural dismantling*: 2Ki 23:15 — Josiah's demolition of the Bethel altar — the physical destruction of the contagious sin's structural legacy points toward the complete eschatological dismantling of all sin-transmitting structures. The typological direction (T0.4.1) points toward a leader whose authority transmits righteousness rather than sin — the eschatological antitype of Jeroboam.

**[CHAR-8]** E — Limited eschatological evidence. 1Ki 12:19 / 2Ch 10:19 — "Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David to this day" — the persistent revolt from the Davidic house names a fracture in the covenant history that the prophetic expectation of a restored Davidic king addresses. The revolt is a wound in the covenant history that remains open "to this day" — pointing forward to a future divine resolution in which the fractured covenant community is restored under the promised Davidic heir. The present revolt anticipates the eschatological re-gathering under Davidic authority.

**[CHAR-9]** E — Yes — in two directions. (1) *Negative eschatological fullness*: Mat 12:31 — the unforgivable blasphemy against the Spirit points toward permanent eschatological consequence — the unforgiven state endures into eternity. VCG-03's beast-blasphemy (Rev 13:5 — "for forty-two months") is explicitly eschatological: the beast's constitutive sinful speech is a feature of the end-times period before divine judgment falls on it. (2) *Positive eschatological direction*: 1Ti 1:13 — Paul's transformation from blasphemer to apostle points toward the eschatological goal — the creature formed toward God's purposes rather than against them. The positive eschatological direction is: sinful speech's reversal is part of the creature's eschatological transformation.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes. The evidence points wickedness-as-settled-person-identity toward an eschatological terminus — but one of dissolution rather than fullness. The eschatological evidence in VCG-05 is concentrated: Psa 9:5 — "you have blotted out their name forever and ever"; Psa 37:10 — "in a little while the wicked will be no more"; Isa 11:4 — "he shall kill the wicked" by the rod of his mouth; Mal 4:3 — "they will be ashes under the soles of your feet on the day when I act"; Dan 12:10 — the wicked "act wickedly" and "cannot understand" in the eschatological purification. The eschatological direction is termination — the characteristic reaches its ultimate consequence in the complete dissolution of the wicked person's existence and legacy. This is an eschatological fullness only in the sense that judgment is fully executed; there is no positive eschatological destiny for the characteristic itself.

**[CHAR-2]** E — The evidence points the characteristic toward an eschatological terminus of separation and judgment rather than positive fullness. Mat 13:49 (vc=14459 — VCG-04): "at the end of the age, the angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous" — the eschatological terminus of the characteristic is separation. 2Ti 3:13 (vc=14451 — VCG-06): "evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse" — the eschatological trajectory is progressive deterioration arriving at its terminus. The characteristic's eschatological fullness is the complete actualisation of its separation from the righteous — the sorting that is already occurring in the present (Joh 3:19-20 — VCG-04: loving darkness) is finalised eschatologically (Mat 13:49).

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes. The characteristic is pointed toward eschatological exclusion as its terminus. Rev 21:27 (vc=22 — VCG-05): "nothing unclean will ever enter it, nor anyone who does what is detestable or false, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life" — the characteristic's eschatological fullness is the complete and final exclusion of the abominable from the divine presence. Rev 17:5 (vc=65878 — VCG-05): Babylon the mother of abominations is the eschatological type of the system that generates and propagates abomination — its end is judgment. The Proverbs antithetical pattern (delight vs. abomination) points toward an eschatological resolution where the distinction is finalised: the abominable are excluded; the delightful (the upright) enter.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. VCG-06 (5V) is the explicitly eschatological evidence: Dan 9:27 (vc=65914 — VCG-06), Dan 11:31 (vc=65915 — VCG-06), Dan 12:11 (vc=65916 — VCG-06) — the abomination of desolation as an eschatological peak-sacrilege event. Mat 24:15 (vc=65876 — VCG-06) and Mar 13:14 (vc=65877 — VCG-06) extend this eschatological reading. The characteristic's eschatological fullness is the abomination-of-desolation event — the maximal expression of idolatrous sacrilege that marks the terminus of the trajectory. Simultaneously, the restoration eschatology: Eze 37:23 (vc=65913 — VCG-05) points toward a future where the characteristic has been completely removed and the covenant relationship fully restored.

**[CHAR-5]** E — Yes. The characteristic is pointed toward eschatological judgment and elimination. Psa 92:7-9 (vc=38246/38247 — VCG-03): "evildoers flourish… doomed to destruction forever… all evildoers shall be scattered" — the "forever" and the certainty of scattering point toward a final elimination of the characteristic. Psa 94:23 (vc=38249 — VCG-03): "wipe them out for their wickedness; the Lord our God will wipe them out" — the final decisive act of divine wiping-out as the eschatological culmination. Psa 101:8 (vc=38226 — VCG-03): "morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land, cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the Lord" — the city of the Lord from which evildoers are permanently excluded is an eschatological vision. The trajectory is toward a future in which the characteristic is entirely absent from the divine community.

**[CHAR-6]** E — Yes. The characteristic is oriented toward eschatological judgment as its trajectory. VCG-01 is itself situated within the eschatological judgment sequence of Revelation 16 — the characteristic's most extreme form occurs within the eschatological framework. Rev 16:9/11/21 (VCG-01): the plagues are the eschatological end-time judgments; the characteristic expressed under these judgments is at the eschatological terminus. Rev 13:6 (vc=14356 — VCG-01): the beast's blasphemy is an eschatological figure at the apex of cosmic anti-God defiance. 1Pe 2:12 (vc=14377 — VCG-03): "glorify God on the day of visitation" — the day of visitation is the eschatological moment when the false accusation is definitively reversed and truth is established.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All six characteristics point toward eschatological judgment and elimination — confirmed unanimously across the cluster. The eschatological trajectories vary in their specific form: Char 1 (Dan 12:10 — "the wicked shall act wickedly and none of the wicked shall understand" — eschatological hardening; Psa 37:10 — "the wicked seen no more"), Char 2 (Mat 13:49 — the evil separated from the righteous at the end of the age), Char 3 (Rev 21:27 — nothing abominable enters the holy city; Rev 17:5 — Babylon the mother of abominations as eschatological type), Char 4 (Dan 9:27 → Mat 24:15 — the abomination of desolation as eschatological peak-sacrilege), Char 5 (Psa 94:23 — "wipe them out"; Psa 92:7 — "doomed to destruction forever"), Char 6 (Rev 13:6 — the beast as the eschatological type of all blasphemy; Rev 16:9/11/21 — the population's final unrepentant state under eschatological judgment). The cluster's eschatological trajectory: six converging lines of inner evil all pointing toward the same eschatological terminus of judgment, elimination, and separation from the holy.

**[CHAR-1]** E — Yes, at two evidenced points. First, the red-heifer remedy (Num 19:9, M10c-A-VCG-07) as a "sin offering" designated for "the congregation of the people of Israel" as a perpetual provision anticipates a permanent resolution beyond what the ritual can provide within the corpus itself — it points to a cleansing economy beyond the current age. Second, the NT categorical revision (Act 10:28, M10c-B-VCG-05) — "what God has made clean, do not call unclean" — is itself an eschatological declaration: the old-covenant categorical system is being transformed by the inbreaking of the new, showing that the current ritual defilement structure is provisional. The present operation of the characteristic is oriented toward a future fullness in which the categories themselves are either fulfilled or transcended.

**[CHAR-2]** E — Yes, explicitly. Rev 3:4 (VCG-05): "people who have not soiled their garments... will walk with me in white, for they are worthy" — the eschatological fullness is walking with Christ in white; the present non-defilement is oriented toward this future state. Rev 14:4 (VCG-05): "redeemed from mankind as firstfruits for God and the Lamb" — the present non-defilement is oriented toward an eschatological identification as firstfruits for God. Isa 35:8 (VCG-05): the Way of Holiness — the "unclean shall not pass over it" — is an eschatological-restorative highway from which the morally unclean are excluded, showing that the eschatological fullness is characterised by the complete absence of the characteristic.

**[CHAR-3]** E — Yes, explicitly and substantially. Three eschatological promises address the characteristic directly. Eze 37:23 (VCG-05): "they shall not defile themselves anymore with their idols and their detestable things, or with any of their transgressions. But I will save them from all the backslidings in which they have sinned, and will cleanse them; and they shall be my people, and I will be their God" — comprehensive eschatological restoration in which the defilement-state is permanently ended. Isa 52:1 (VCG-05): "there shall no more come into you the uncircumcised and the unclean" — the holy city permanently excludes the defiling condition. Zec 13:1 (VCG-05): "a fountain opened for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, to cleanse them from sin and uncleanness" — the divinely provided fountain of permanent cleansing.

**[CHAR-4]** E — Yes. (1) Mar 9:25 (VCG-01): "never enter him again" — the command against re-entry points toward an eschatological fullness in which such spirits have no permanent access to persons. (2) Mat 12:43/Luk 11:24 (VCG-02) — the spirit "passing through waterless places seeking rest, and finding none" — implies an eschatological state in which the spirit finds no place of rest at all, its domain permanently eliminated. The present expulsions are anticipations of the final comprehensive defeat of all adversarial spiritual powers.

**[CLUSTER]** E — All four characteristics are E on eschatological orientation. Characteristic 1: the red-heifer provision as a "sin offering" anticipating a deeper cleansing economy, and the Act 10:28 categorical revision as an eschatological declaration of the old-covenant categorical system's transformation. Characteristic 2: explicitly eschatological — Rev 3:4 (walking with Christ in white), Rev 14:4 (firstfruits for God and the Lamb), Isa 35:8 (the Way of Holiness excluding the unclean). Characteristic 3: the most extensively developed — Eze 37:23 (permanent non-defilement and covenant formula restored), Isa 52:1 (holy city permanently excluding the unclean), Zec 13:1 (the cleansing fountain). Characteristic 4: Mar 9:25's command "never enter him again" and the spirit's post-expulsion restlessness implying a future state where it finds no habitation. The cluster's unanimous eschatological orientation confirms M10c as a domain that is not self-contained but oriented toward a fullness in which all four registers of defilement are definitively overcome. The M10c domain is designed to end.

questions.question_text: What does the present experience of this characteristic anticipate about its future fullness?

findings.session_b_note:
Drawing from the partial evidence:

**Present forgiveness anticipates complete relational restoration:** Jer 31:34 — the new covenant's "remember no more" and "they shall all know me" together name a state of complete, unmediated, unimpeded knowing of God made possible by forgiveness. The present experience of forgiveness (partial knowing, renewed access) anticipates this fullness — a state in which the forgiven relationship with God is without remainder, without barrier, without residual guilt.

**Present forgiveness anticipates redemption completed:** Psa 130:8 — "he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities." The present experience of forgiveness for specific sins anticipates a comprehensive future redemption — not merely specific instances forgiven but "all iniquities" addressed. The present is partial; the future is complete.

**Present horizontal forgiveness anticipates restored community:** The structural logic of the forgiveness commands (Mat 18:35; Mar 11:25; Luk 17:4) — forgiving within the community as a practice — anticipates a community in which the relational ruptures caused by sin are permanently resolved. The present practice is formation toward a future state of community wholeness.

*New finding:* The present forgiveness experience functions as a **threefold eschatological anticipation**: (1) of complete relational knowing of God without barrier; (2) of comprehensive redemption without remainder; (3) of community wholeness without relational rupture. This threefold structure has not been assembled in existing observations.

findings.session_b_note:
From the available evidence:

**Present splanchnizō anticipates the fullness of divine compassion enacted without constraint.** The Synoptic compassion-movements operate within the constraints of the present age — limited by what healing can accomplish, by what one meal can provide, by the finitude of the encounter. The eschatological fullness anticipated is a compassion that acts without these constraints — where the gut-stirring of God-in-Christ toward human need finds its complete expression.

**Present sumpaschō anticipates syndoxazō.** The present experience of suffering-with is incomplete — it is the experience of solidarity in suffering, not yet in glory. The future fullness anticipated is the transformation of the shared suffering into shared glory: compassion-solidarity arriving at its eschatological destination.

**Present chesed anticipates its own inexhaustibility.** The daily renewal of chesed (Lam 3:23 — "new every morning") anticipates a fullness in which the renewal is no longer needed because the reality is complete and uninterrupted. Present chesed is the foretaste of an inexhaustible compassion-love that requires no renewal because it is permanently full.

**What is missing (P):** The data does not address what the human person's compassion looks like in its eschatological fullness — whether the human capacity for compassion is itself transformed, expanded, or completed in the age to come. The eschatological anthropology of compassion is a gap for Session D; SD-012 covers the sumpaschō dimension but not the wider question.

findings.session_b_note:
**Present divine nature participation anticipates full divine likeness:** 2Pe 1:4 — the present *becoming* a partaker of divine nature is not the fullness; it is the entry. The future fullness would be the complete realisation of that participation without the present constraint of corruption.

**Present fellowship of sufferings anticipates resurrection:** Phili 3:10-11 — the fellowship entered through suffering and death anticipates the resurrection as its completion. What is now entered through pain and death will be completed in the resurrection-mode of fellowship.

**Present hope anticipates the removal of what grounds fear:** Ecc 9:4 — the fellowship that grounds hope in the present is a fellowship *with the living*. The eschatological fullness would be fellowship that is no longer threatened by death — the mortal fellowship of the living being completed in an immortal fellowship.

**New finding:** The present experience of fellowship in every register is presented as partial and forward-facing: participation is entered but not yet complete; hope is grounded but not yet fulfilled; suffering-fellowship is entered but resurrection is not yet fully realised. Fellowship is constitutively *not yet* at its highest registers — it is oriented toward a fullness it is moving into. This is a structural feature of the characteristic assembled for the first time here.

findings.finding_value: Reading T5 as a whole reveals mercy's formative character: it is not static but inherently developmental and generative. The T5 synthesis: mercy produces dual transformation (objective condition + subjective orientation simultaneously); it moves persons through named inner-state sequences (at least four distinct sequences, Q&A-128); its mechanism is always specific, embodied, and costly; suffering is both the context that generates mercy-seeking and the formation-medium through which mercy-capacity deepens (Q&A-135); mercy functions as the first and foundational inner garment in the character formation sequence (Q&A-138); and mercy has an eschatological trajectory (future fullness in which the mercy-relationship is complete and permanent). T5.7 closed (no constitutional body deposit). The overarching T5 finding: mercy is a characteristic that is received, then forms the person into one who can receive it more deeply and extend it more genuinely — it has an inherent developmental arc.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTER-111-027: T5's eschatological trajectory (mercy pointing toward fullness) and T7's primary anchor verse (Psa 78:38 — the verse that most fully encodes the mercy-event) are related in that Psa 78:38's causal seq…
findings.finding_value: T5's eschatological trajectory (mercy pointing toward fullness) and T7's primary anchor verse (Psa 78:38 — the verse that most fully encodes the mercy-event) are related in that Psa 78:38's causal sequence (compassion → atoning act → anger-restraint → wrath-modulation) is a historical instance of the formative arc T5 describes — it is the sequence mercy worked in Israel's history under the old covenant, pointing toward the completed mercy of the new covenant (Heb 8:12 — T5's eschatological trajectory). T7's vocabulary arc (Q&A-180) is the lexical narrative of T5's developmental arc: the vocabulary moves from inner generative care (racham root) through mechanism (kipper root) through reception-posture (techinah) — which is the same sequence as T5's receive → mechanism → formation → eschatological trajectory.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-023-005: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's stan…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces three inter-related formation findings. First, transformation is evidenced in both modes simultaneously (Luke 15:20-24 — the father's compassion produces condition-change in the son's standing AND orientation-change in his reception of identity). Second, the formative cycle is self-reinforcing: the after-state of compassion-received feeds back into the before-state of compassion-readiness in the future — the person who has received compassion becomes more capable of extending it. Third, compassion plays a dual role in the sanctification arc: it is simultaneously the character target being formed (the person becoming compassionate over time) and the motivational ground that makes the formative relationship survivable through failure and return. Matthew 18:27 introduces the most critical formative warning: received compassion can be forfeited by failure to extend it — compassion is not a permanently possessed gift but a participatory moral framework. Three distinct mechanisms of change operate across contexts: encounter/sudden (splanchnizō — the moment of being moved), covenantal-sustaining/gradual (chesed — the steady faithfulness over time), and participatory-ontological (2Pe 1:4 pattern — sharing in what God is). T5.7 is formally closed: no body deposit established. All four relationships between suffering and compassion are evidenced — suffering reveals, tests, deepens, and produces compassion.

findings.session_b_note: Cited as source by SYN-INTRA-068-005: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outp…
findings.finding_value: T5 produces the richest formation account of any characteristic in the review set. Five mechanisms of change are distinguished: encounter (specific relational event — Luk 1:28, Ruth 2:10), spirit-outpouring (Zec 12:10), word (Act 20:32 — grace operating through the proclaimed word), inference (Rom 8:32 — cognitive reasoning from the supreme grace-event to present assurance), and mediated-transformation (grace → tenderheartedness → forgiving — Eph 4:32, SD030). Five distinct mechanisms for a single characteristic is unique in the programme data. The creaturely recognition response (fear → mourning → prostration) is confirmed as a consistent transitional state in all grace-sequences across different evidential contexts — not incidental detail but structural feature. Suffering's relationship to grace is precisely distinguished: grace inhabits suffering rather than suffering producing grace (2Cor 12:9 — weakness as theatre of grace, not as generator of grace). The reversibility question (T5.1 P2) is the most significant gap: not fully resolved. The eschatological trajectory (T5.6) is evidenced through Eph 2:7 ("the immeasurable riches of his grace in the coming ages") and charitoō's perfect-passive form (completed state with continuing effect). T2.8 remains open; T5.7 is formally left open accordingly.

This is partially realised in the present (believers know God through the Spirit) but fully realised only eschatologically when the partial knowing gives way to complete and unmediated knowing. (2) Universal and eternal belonging — the present covenant of belonging ("I will be their God and they shall be my people" — Heb 8:10 — OBS-034-059) anticipates its eschatological fullness: "the dwelling of God is with man. He will dwell with them and they will be his people" (Rev 21:3 context — OBS-034-063 direction). The covenant formula reaches its fullest expression in the new creation. (3) Healed creation — the Noahic covenant's universal scope (all living creatures — OBS-034-038) anticipates the new creation's universal scope (new heaven and earth — OBS-034-063). Covenant moves from promise to realisation, from partial to total, from temporal to eternal.

findings.finding_value: Present grace is a foretaste of "immeasurable riches" (Eph 2:7): what is now received partially and experientially will be displayed in its full extent. The grace-sphere (888-002 — "this grace in which we stand") is a present experience of what will be fully constituted. The irrevocability of charismata (1301-001 — Rom 11:29) anticipates a permanence that is eschatologically grounded. Present ra.tsah (divine acceptance) anticipates the eschatological "there I will accept them" (Eze 20:40) — full and unrestricted acceptance.
